# PREFACE.

->Greetings to those Readers who deign to read prefaces!<-

Before I send you, **Kind Reader** <note>original: *B. Lector* (Benevole Lector); a common polite greeting in 17th and 18th-century books</note>, to the reading of this little book itself, I have judged that certain points should be mentioned beforehand. *One* concerns the subject matter itself; the *other* concerns the method of handling it. I confess that more than once the saying of the **Poet** came to the reader’s mind: *Into the fire with you—you papers* <note>original: *Ite in ignem -- chartæ*; a sentiment similar to that found in Martial or Catullus, expressing frustration with bad or useless writing</note>, especially since I have always applied myself with all my strength to reading only the best writers.

Yet these things did not prevent me from bringing the **little book** <term>libellum (similar to opusculum, meaning a small book)</term> to a conclusion and swallowing some of the annoyance. I have always thought, and still think, that those who apply their minds to writing should strive above all to ensure that what they write is useful and will be profitable. It is not a question of how pleasant the labor is, but how useful it is to the Reader. If anywhere, certainly here that saying of the **Poet** has a place: *Unless what we do is useful, our glory is foolish* <note>original: *Nisi utile est quod facimus, stulta est gloria*; a quote from the Roman fabulist Phaedrus</note>. Moreover, I believe that those trifles which I recount—albeit unwillingly—lead to serious matters. How this is so must now be shown. anyone aware of the times in which we live will call it into doubt; that nothing is more useful and necessary than for the *Truth* and *divinity of the Christian Religion* to be proved by the most solid arguments, and defended against any insults of the *Wicked* and the *Unbelievers*. ...Indeed, being in Naples myself in the month of March of the year 1726, I had the opportunity in the Church of San Giovanni a Carbonara <note>A prominent 14th-century Gothic church in Naples.</note> to see what is presented as being the blood of **St. John the Baptist**. What I can sincerely assert is that the thickened liquid enclosed within seemed to me anything but blood; but rather a kind of solidified oil or ointment to which a reddish color had been given, which even imitated that of blood very poorly. But what absurdity can one not persuade people to believe, who seem to believe with unwavering certainty <note>original: "dur comme fer," literally "hard as iron."</note> that a marble statue caught the Plague, that a part of its face is still swollen from it, and that one can currently discover on its right cheek the mark that the bubo <term>bubon: a swollen lymph node symptomatic of the bubonic plague</term> left there upon receding? Indeed, being myself in Naples in the month of *March* of the year 1726, I had the opportunity in the Church of *St. John Carbonara* <note>San Giovanni a Carbonara, a famous Gothic church in Naples.</note> to see what is presented as the blood of *St. John the Baptist*. What I can sincerely assure is that the thickened liquid enclosed within appeared to me to be anything but blood; rather, it seemed a type of condensed oil or ointment to which a reddish color had been given—one that imitated blood very poorly indeed.

But what absurdity can one not persuade people of, who seem to believe, with absolute certainty, <note>Literally "hard as iron."</note> that a marble statue caught the Plague, that a part of its face is still swollen from it, and that one can currently discover on its right cheek the mark that the Bubo left when it broke? <note>A bubo is the painfully swollen lymph node characteristic of the bubonic plague. But according to *Pâris* himself, the *Pope* is *inspired* by God and is the *Infallible judge* of controversies; therefore, God cannot confirm with miracles a doctrine which He has most solemnly condemned through the mouth of the *Infallible* judge and Christ's Legate on earth.

From this it follows that certain Catholics often, under the pretext of not falling for the "simplicity" (as they call it) of olden times, abandon to the Heretics those miracles which, though they are not articles of faith, are no less proven. *...the place after having cowardly abandoned the outskirts.* <note>This sentence fragment completes the quote from the Jesuit on the previous page.</note> Thus said that Jesuit. To these things, I reply with the following:

1st. We concede that in matters regarding Religion, one must act with seriousness; and that those who break out into laughter and quips without further delay—especially when they cannot sufficiently understand the nature and character of divine things—act rashly. In this way, we disapprove of the jokes and taunts of the *Unbelievers*, with which they receive the Christian Religion (supported and demonstrated as it is by so many arguments) either without examination or by criticizing it because of certain opinions that are difficult for the human intellect to grasp. For it is tasteless and foreign to reason to explode with laughter at that which we do not sufficiently understand, especially when it has been put forward by *the best and wisest men*.

# AN EXERCISE ON THE ORIGIN AND AUTHORITY OF MIRACLES,

->Which are attributed to Pythagoras, Apollonius of Tyana, Francis of Assisi, Dominic, and Ignatius Loyola,<-

## CHAPTER I.

### The Occasion and Scope of the Exercise.

As I have reflected and considered more than once by what means it has come to pass that many men—not lacking in talent and judgment—have leaned toward **Atheism** <term>Atheismus: in this period, the term was often used broadly to describe not just a denial of God's existence, but any belief system that undermined established religious authority</term>, that most serious and pestilential error; many and various causes have appeared before my mind, all of which the nature of my current plan does not allow me to recount here. Among those causes, **Superstition and frauds in matters regarding Religion** stand out above all others. Superstition so dulls and suppresses the power of right reason that those who are struck by this unlucky star <note>original: *infausto hoc sydere adflati sunt*. An astrological metaphor meaning to be influenced or "breathed upon" by an evil omen or planetary alignment.</note> are prone to the most foolish—

He specifically targets the "miracles" of ancient figures like Pythagoras and Catholic founders like Ignatius Loyola as examples of such deception.</summary>

—most foolish things to be believed, and are most prompt and ready to stubbornly defend them. For once the authority of reason has been shaken off, there is nothing so absurd or dull that the blind hearts of men will not greedily seize upon it. Indeed, they sometimes progress to such a level of madness that they kiss <note>original: *deosculentur*. They glory in that very stupidity and rest sweetly within it.

The more these superstitious people rave and admire such childish follies, the more this most empty error strikes the eyes of others, and it vehemently offends all those who have not declared war on reason. For however great the unhappiness of the ages may have been, or the ignorance and blindness of men, it still could not bring it about that everyone—as if a mist had been drawn over their minds—should be utterly blinded and bewitched.

# CHAPTER II.
## *Concerning Miracles in General.*

Those who recorded the lives of those Men whom we just mentioned believed it to be their primary task to prove that God performed very many and numerous miracles in their favor. For they believed that the disbelief of mortals could hardly be addressed in any other way. However, since the minds of people today are not easily led to accept miracles without the most weighty reasons, let the writers of those lives grant something to the boldness <note>The author refers to the growing skepticism and critical inquiry of the Enlightenment era.</note> of our age, and allow us to inspect those miracles a little more closely. It is certainly a matter of no small importance to admit or not admit a certain miracle; it is dangerous both to believe and not to believe. 

If those who have separated from the Roman Church <note>A reference to Protestants and the Reformation.</note> boasted of miracles performed in favor of the religion they profess, there is no doubt that those who disagree with us would examine them with the most inquisitive eyes; nor could we justly blame them for that. It is only fair that they grant the same to us. 

Unlike the Unbelievers <term>Incredulis: those who reject the possibility of the supernatural</term>, we do not categorize miracles among the unknown laws of nature. We think so nobly and magnificently of God that we firmly believe nothing that falls within human understanding, or which is called "possible," exceeds His strength and power. At the same time, however, we are so convinced of the Holiness, Wisdom, and Goodness of the Divine <term>Numinis: the divine power, will, or presence of God</term> that God would not produce unusual portents without the weightiest reasons, and that He [confirms] <note>The sentence continues on the next page.</note> only the holiest things,

...will confirm. But before we inquire whether the miracles attributed to **Pythagoras**, **Francis**, etc., were truly performed, we must say something beforehand about miracles in general, especially since we must diligently investigate for what purpose they were produced. As far as I know, there are **three opinions** held by **the learned concerning miracles**.

Some reject <note>original: *explodunt*, meaning to hiss a bad actor off a stage</note> all miracles and pass off unknown laws of nature as miracles. They claim that fraudulent men, in order to keep the common people in their duty <note>That is, to keep them obedient to religious or civil authority.</note>, ascribed things that follow from the necessary laws of nature to the command and will of Almighty God. In this way **Spinoza** behaved foolishly, as have others after him; however, we will not linger in refuting this opinion (since it has been done abundantly by others), especially because it contributes nothing to clarifying the present dispute. 

Others think that "true" miracles can be performed not only by God, but also by angels—both good and evil. They believe that God and good angels perform miracles to prove and confirm saving truth, while evil spirits <term>Genios: spirits or supernatural beings, often used here to refer to demons</term> establish errors and superstition by producing portents. Many theologians hold this opinion; among the more recent, **Locke**, **Clarke**, **Le Clerc**, and others are prominent. 

Finally, the third opinion is held by those who attribute the power of performing miracles to God alone. They believe all other things held as miracles were fabricated by impostors; they utterly deny that such things can be performed by the Devil. This opinion was followed by the famous and most learned theologians **Ch. Nolten** in a special dissertation, **Alphonse Turretin** in his exquisite work *On the Truth of the Christian Religion*, and most recently and at great length by **Du Serces**, a theologian of the **Anglican Church**. Although it matters little to our purpose,

It therefore had to be proved that God intended for that entire system of laws to be regarded as divine.

I know that the **Dissenters** <note>Those who believe that beings other than God, such as demons, can perform true miracles.</note>, in order to prove their opinion, appeal to certain passages of the **Sacred Scriptures**. Whatever the case may be, it is certain that the theology of the **Egyptian priests** consisted of impostures and troublesome trifles rather than true wisdom or the power to perform unusual miracles. 

Hence, in the *Questions to the Orthodox*—a work added to the writings of **Justin Martyr**—the wisdom of the Egyptians is called **"a wisdom teaching the doctrines of error"** <note>original Greek: σοφία διδάσκουσα τὰ τῆς πλάνης διδάγματα</note>. And this seems to have been the reason why **Moses**, when mentioning the stupendous miracles of God, did not explain at length what the nature was of the works produced by the **Magi**. I do not doubt that Moses, as well as the wiser among the Israelites, clearly understood what the arts of those men <note>The Egyptian magicians or sorcerers.</note> consisted of. But *Learned Men* <note>A reference to the scholars mentioned on the previous page, Shuckford and Canz, who argued for the reality of these miracles.</note> say that the question is not about the titles and the craft of those men, but whether they produced miracles in the true sense of the word. They claim this is evident from the fact that Moses testifies in the clearest words that those Magicians turned their staffs into serpents, changed water into blood, and finally, that frogs were brought forth at their command.

I respond, therefore, in the second place, that it is not at all likely that these wonders are to be attributed either to *God* or to the *Devil*. The *most learned Canz* <note>Israel Gottlieb Canz (1690–1753), a German philosopher and theologian.</note> himself concedes that they cannot be attributed to God; for such an action would not be consistent with either the wisdom or the goodness of God. But the same reasoning persuades me to believe that these things were not the work of the Devil. 

For why would the Best Divinity <note>original: *Optimum Numen*</note> have permitted that, at the very time when His infinite power was to be demonstrated as greatly as possible, the Devil should thwart <note>original: *sufflaminaret* — literally "to clog the wheels," meaning to hinder or obstruct.</note> His efforts and lead men to suspect that Moses, just like the Magicians, was either an impostor or was equipped with the same power for performing miracles? Let us consider what difficulties Pharaoh himself, and many others who saw these things with their own eyes, would have been thrown into. 

3. Is it a greater miracle to create lice than to change a staff into a living serpent? Certainly, if the Devil is as wise and as powerful <note>original: *patens*, likely an error in the original or transcription for *potens* (powerful).</note> as the *Learned Men* contend, I do not see the reason why he would not have demonstrated his power on this occasion. The *illustrious Le Clerc* <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous theologian and biblical scholar.</note> himself rightly observed this difficulty...

## CHAPTER III.

### *The principal miracles of Pythagoras and Apollonius are related.*

After we have explained our opinion on the origin of miracles in a few words, it is time for us to approach and look a little more closely at those miracles which are commonly attributed to Pythagoras and the others whom we promised to discuss in the title of this booklet. In this chapter, without further investigation, we will relate the portents produced—if it pleases the Gods—by Pythagoras and Apollonius. In the following sections, we shall judge their authority and the value of the witnesses. Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose biography of Pythagoras is a primary source for these legends.</note> has such an exalted view of Pythagoras's philosophy that he declares it extends even to the instruction of brute animals. In Chapter 13 of *The Life of Pythagoras*, Küster’s edition <note>Ludolf Küster (1670–1716) was a noted German scholar; his 1707 edition of Iamblichus was the standard scholarly text at the time.</note>, he says: *For Pythagoras detained the Daunian Bear, which was most severely troubling the inhabitants, as they say <note>original: "NB." - a Latin abbreviation for "nota bene," used here to highlight that even the ancient source expresses some hesitation with "as they say."</note>, and for a long enough time he stroked it with his hand; and having revived it with barley-cakes and fruits from trees, and having bound it by an oath never to touch living things again, he let it go. It truly hid itself immediately in the mountains and woods, and thereafter it was not seen to [attack] any cattle...*

it is permitted to set this forth; it is necessary that we skillfully investigate, partly for what purpose those miracles were brought forth, and partly by what character those individuals were adorned who were endowed with such unusual gifts. Once this has finally been explored, we may incline our judgment toward one side or the other. Let us therefore consider the teaching of Pythagoras, and his nature and character, according to the narrative of the biographers <note>original Greek: βιογραφων (biographōn)</note> who have extolled those Heroes with the highest praises, as they deserve. And indeed, having immediately changed his wife's name from Parthenis to Pythais—after both his son and the Delphic prophetess—he named the infant himself (who was soon born in Sidon, Phoenicia) Pythagoras: signifying, of course, that he had been foretold to him by the Pythian <note>The "Pythian" refers to the god Apollo, to whom the Oracle at Delphi was dedicated.</note>. ...from the truth that the birth of *Pythagoras* was considered an unusual miracle. From this, it is clear upon what foundation the narrative of *Iamblichus* and *Porphyry* was built <note>Iamblichus and Porphyry were Neoplatonist philosophers of the 3rd and 4th centuries AD who wrote highly idealized and miraculous accounts of Pythagoras's life.</note>. Moreover, his long stay in *Egypt* and his close interaction with the *Priests* of that region did much to corrupt the character of *Pythagoras*. For it is well known that no nation was more inclined to foster foolish opinions than the *Egyptians*, and that their entire religion consisted of difficult trifles—so much so that *Dacier* <note>André Dacier (1651–1722), whose laudatory biography of Pythagoras was criticized by more skeptical Enlightenment scholars.</note> is worthy of laughter rather than refutation, when on page three of his *Life of Pythagoras* he calls the learning of the *Egyptians* "the true wisdom" <note>original French: *la veritable ſageſſe*</note>; whereas one might rather call it "true charlatanry" <note>original French: *une veritable Charlatanerie*</note>. For by emblems and figures (about which we are speaking here), the minds of men are perverted, and the *impulses of the imagination* are increased rather than a clear knowledge of things. Proceeding along this path, *Pythagoras* finally fell into fanaticism. At least it will be established by more than one example that his mind was deceived and corrupted by vain images, a process to which the *Egyptian* method of philosophizing undoubtedly contributed much. In vain, therefore, did *Pythagoras* believe that if he frequented *Egypt*, "he would be the most divine and the wisest of all men" <note>original Greek: θειότατον ἑαυτὸν καὶ σοφώτατον ὑπὲρ ἅπαντας ἔσεσθαι ἀνθρώπους</note>, becoming wiser and more divine than all other mortals. In this very workshop of wisdom, *Iamblichus* says on page 11: "He did not endure such things out of superstition, as one might simply suppose; but much more from a love and desire for contemplation and piety, so that nothing worth learning, preserved in the secrets or rites of the gods, should escape him" <note>original Greek: οὐχὶ δαισιδαιμονίας ἕνεκα τὸ τοιοῦτον ὑπομείνας, ὡς ἄν τις ἁπλῶς ὑπολάβοι. Πολὺ δὲ μᾶλλον ἔρωτι καὶ ἐρέξει θεωρίας καὶ εὐλαβείας, ἵνα μήτι αὐτὸν τῶν ἀξιομαθήτων διαλάθῃ ἐν θεῶν ἀπορρήτοις ἢ τελεταῖς φυλαττόμενα</note>. From this it certainly appears that *Pythagoras* sought after whatever was extraordinary <note>original Greek: τερατῶδες (teratodes), which can mean "miraculous" but also "monstrous" or "absurd."</note> and unusual.

It is well known that he [Pythagoras] asserted that his own mind had wandered through many bodies over a long period of time. According to the testimony of *Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote a famous biography of Pythagoras.</note> (chapter 14, page 48) and *Porphyry* <note>Another Neoplatonist biographer of Pythagoras.</note>—to say nothing of others—he would remind many of those who enjoyed his friendship, by clear and manifest signs, of their *former lives, which their souls had already completed long ago, before being bound to this body.* He demonstrated through certain and indubitable signs that he himself *had been Euphorbus, the son of Panthous, who defeated Patroclus.* <note>In the *Iliad*, Euphorbus is the Trojan warrior who first wounded Patroclus, the companion of Achilles. Pythagoras famously claimed he recognized Euphorbus's shield hanging in a temple at Argos.</note>

Who does not see from this that this man was either out of his mind <note>original: "mente captum"</note> or foolishly arrogant? If he had said that he *conjectured* from certain signs that his mind had once inhabited the body of *Euphorbus*, there would be no reason for us to wonder greatly, for we know what ignorance and mental weakness can sometimes achieve. Thus the most ingenious *Locke* <note>John Locke (1632–1704), the English philosopher who discussed the nature of the soul and identity in his *Essay Concerning Human Understanding*.</note> mentions a certain man, by no means unlearned, who believed that his body was occupied by the mind that had been in *Socrates*. But since he promised to demonstrate with clear evidence not only that he was once *Euphorbus*, but also whose bodies the souls of others had inhabited, he deserved to be sent to *Anticyra*. <note>A Greek town famous for hellebore, a plant used in antiquity to treat insanity. > *O wonderful and singular memory of Pythagoras! O wretched forgetfulness of all the rest of us, who do not know who we were before! Clearly, a vain old man (just as idle old women are wont to do) fashioned fables as if for gullible infants.*

...the vanity of a most frivolous man. There follows another mark, and one especially indicative of stupidity and pride. For the sake of brevity, let *Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote a famous biography of Pythagoras.</note> alone be heard (page 51):

*When the disciples rose from bed, they would shake off the nocturnal sluggishness, relaxation, and lethargy by means of certain songs and melodies composed in a peculiar manner, which were performed either by the stroke of the lyre alone or even by the voice. But for himself, that man [Pythagoras] did not provide such things through instruments and the voice in the same way; rather, through a certain ineffable divinity that is difficult for the intellect to grasp, he would strain his ears and fix his mind upon the more sublime harmonies of the world. And he alone, as it appeared, perceived with his hearing and intellect the universal harmony and consonance of the Spheres and the Stars moved through them. These produced a song far more perfect than what is common among mortals, and one that could be heard without ever becoming tiresome. Through unlike and variously diverse vibrations* <note>original: "stridores"</note>*, with speeds, magnitudes, and motions arranged according to a certain musical ratio, they produced a revolution and a circular motion that was at once most pleasing and beautiful in various ways. Having been, as it were, watered by this, and well-composed and nourished* <note>original: "saginatus," literally "fattened"</note> *in his mental faculty, he himself thought to display certain images of these things to his disciples, and to imitate them as much as possible, primarily through instruments and also the voice alone.*

*Porphyry* <note>Another Neoplatonist biographer of Pythagoras.</note> testifies to the same (Section 30). Indeed, Pythagoras must have been all ears to have heard that harmony of the Planets! Perhaps, however, the Gods—among whose number he himself was reckoned—are equipped with very long ears. <note>A mocking reference comparing Pythagoras to a donkey, a traditional symbol of folly.</note> In the future, I will gladly believe those who say they understand the voices of fleas.

The Prelate Brientis <note>Likely referring to a specific scholar or ecclesiastical authority of the period.</note> criticized Pythagoras because he claimed to perceive the most pleasant harmony of the celestial bodies with his own ears. It is already well known that Pythagoras spoke at length regarding the harmony of the entire world and the celestial bodies; however, I strongly doubt whether he ever actually asserted—or persuaded his followers—that he perceived the sounds of these celestial bodies with his ears. Nor does any ancient writer come to mind who recorded such a thing about Pythagoras. This is what that author argues.

Yet here, in addition to Porphyry, stands Iamblichus. Both testify in the clearest terms that our subject perceived the sound of the celestial bodies with both his ears and his mind, and that this sound most sweetly soothed his ears. Porphyry says: <note>original: "αὐτὸς τῆς τοῦ παντὸς ἁρμονίας ἠκροᾶτο"</note> "He himself listened to the harmony of the universe." If he had intended to say nothing more than that he had observed, guided by reason, that some harmony existed among the celestial bodies, no one would have been particularly surprised. 

Compare the observations of Küster <note>Ludolf Küster (1670–1716), a noted scholar who edited the works of Iamblichus.</note> on this point; moreover, the things that immediately follow testify that Pythagoras attributed something quite extraordinary to himself. For he believed (as Iamblichus continues) that to him alone among all who dwell upon the earth was it granted to understand and hear the sounds of the voice emitted by the universe, and this from the very source and root of nature itself. 

Accordingly, he judged himself worthy to be taught and to learn, and to be assimilated to the celestial beings by striving after and imitating them; inasmuch as he had been so fashioned by a <term>Daemon</term> <note>In the Platonic and Pythagorean tradition, a "Daemon" is a guiding spirit or intermediary divinity, not a malevolent "demon."</note> inspiring him. However, he thought it sufficient for other men to gaze upon him and his gifts, and to improve and be corrected by his images and examples, since they could not truly grasp the primary Archetypes <note>In this context, "Archetypes" refers to the original, perfect forms or mathematical patterns of which the physical world is a mere reflection.</note> of the things themselves. 

It is obvious to everyone that Pythagoras wished to be counted among the gods <term>Superis</term> <note>Literally "those above," referring to the celestial or divine beings.</note> so that he might gain authority for his absurd visions. Hence, his mind was supposedly fashioned by a spirit. Hence, he claimed to grasp the Archetypes of all things...

...they might flee from their own discipline. Who, while reading these things, can restrain themselves from *laughter*? Regarding what should be judged of that **golden thigh**, *Scholars* go in different directions. I would believe it was a pure *imposture* of *Pythagoras*. For why, with witnesses removed, did he show it to *Abaris* alone, if it was to be shown to all as a sign of a heavenly mission? Indeed, *Plutarch in his Life of Numa* <note>Plutarch was a Greek biographer; Numa Pompilius was the legendary second king of Rome, often associated with Pythagorean wisdom</note> testifies that he exhibited it at the Olympic games—that is, in a very great assembly and crowd—to be seen; however, this can hardly be accepted without the testimony of others. Whatever the case may be, if he thought such a thigh had been given to him *from heaven*, he was *insane*; if he faked it, he was an *impostor*.

Let attention be paid meanwhile to what Pythagoras concludes from this: clearly, Pythagoras has a golden thigh; therefore, he is that Apollo whom the **Hyperboreans** <note>In Greek mythology, a race of giants who lived in a land of perfect sunshine "beyond the North Wind"</note> worship as a God. For if a perpetual **transmigration** <note>The Pythagorean belief in the "metempsychosis," where a soul moves into a new body after death</note> from one body into another takes place, how could he see souls thrust down into **Tartarus** <note>The deep abyss in Greek mythology used as a place of punishment for the wicked</note> and chastised with punishments? A liar must have a good memory.

nothing so *impious*, *absurd*, or *detestable*; no *Religion* or rather *superstition* so *foolish* and insulting to God could be devised, that it would not be defended with hands and feet <note>original: "manibus pedibusque"; a Latin idiom meaning "with all one's might" or "by any means necessary."</note>. But this precept was the very first in the *Theology of Pythagoras*. The second, which yields nothing in its absurdity to the first, was: *that God can do all things, even contradictory things*. Iamblichus, page 117: <note>original Greek: "οὐ γὰρ εἶναι τὰ μὲν δυνατὰ τοῖς θεοῖς, τὰ δὲ ἀδύνατα, ὥσπερ οἴεσθαι τοὺς σοφιζομένους, ἀλλὰ πάντα δυνατά."</note> *For it is not the case that some things are possible for the gods and others impossible, as the sophists think, but rather all things are possible.* Truly, when the petty priests <note>The author uses "sacrificuli," a derogatory term for those who perform sacrifices, likely targeting Roman Catholic clergy of his own day by comparison.</note> lie so splendidly that their most foul nonsense can be felt even by the touch, they are accustomed to protect themselves with this *foolish sentiment*, which usually deceives the ignorant but provokes laughter from the attentive. This is a well-known argument to the defenders of *Transubstantiation* <note>The Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the actual body and blood of Christ, which critics argued violated the laws of logic/physics.</note>. The *saying of the Sexton of Cologne* is also well known <note>A reference to a popular anecdote about a simple-minded or stubbornly faithful churchwarden who insisted God could perform even logical impossibilities.</note>. 

But let us briefly run through *Pythagorean Theology*. The Famous and *Most Learned Brucker* <note>Jacob Brucker (1696–1770), a foundational historian of philosophy often cited in the 18th century.</note> depicts it in his own manner—that is, *learnedly and solidly*, to say nothing of others—in the second part of his *History of Philosophy*. I do not wish to vindicate *Pythagoras* here from the charge of *Atheism* with many words, as I have addressed this concern elsewhere. *Justin Martyr* testifies in *On Monarchy* (page 105) and *Exhortation to the Greeks* (page 18) that *Pythagoras* admitted a *Ruler* of the World—that is, one who is eternal, most wise, most powerful, etc. *Clement of Alexandria* says the same in *Stromata*, Book 4, page 477. Hierocles, almost at the beginning of his commentary on the *Golden Verses of Pythagoras*, says that he recognized the only Creator God <note>original Greek: "τὸν Δημιουργικὸν μόνον θεὸν"</note>, whom one might properly call the God of gods, and the highest and best God <note>original Greek: "θεὸν θεῶν κυρίως ἂν εἴποι τις, καὶ θεὸν ὕπατον καὶ ἄριστον"</note>. As is well known, he called this same being the *Monad* <note>original Greek: "μοναδα"; in Pythagorean thought, the "One" or the absolute unity from which all numbers and the universe originate.</note>. *Iamblichus*, in his *Life of Pythagoras* (page 147), is the author—to say nothing of others—for the fact that he believed in God's provident care over all things. Furthermore, he says he considered the rule of the Gods to be the most effective thing for establishing justice...

<meta>This page continues the examination of Pythagoras’s philosophical system. ->❁ ) 63 ( ❁<-

Pythagoras held this to be the case, and he applied it like a principle for establishing the **Republic**, its laws, and justice, according to the standard of right. Nor would it be out of place to add specifically what thoughts he defined as necessary to conceive regarding the **Divine Power** <note>original: "Numen"; a term for the divine will or presence.</note>; namely, that it exists, and that it conducts itself toward the human race in such a way that it watches over them and by no means neglects them. The **Pythagoreans**, having been instructed by him, believed this teaching contained the greatest utility. For they held that we have need of such a **Governance** <note>original: "regimine"</note> which we can in no way resist: and that such is the **Governance of God**, who, since He is so great, is also worthy to command all things. For it was rightly said by them that this animal [man] is by nature prone to insolence, and likewise varied by inclinations, desires, and other passions; and therefore had need of such eminence and oversight from which moderation and order might proceed.

Indeed, they thought that everyone, being conscious of their own natural changeableness, should never forget piety and divine worship. Instead, they should constantly set the **Divine Power** before their mind, as one who observes the actions of men and watches over them without ceasing. He acknowledged the human mind to be **immortal**, or rather incapable of being destroyed; yet, in the meantime, he foully stained this most weighty truth with the foolish opinion of *metempsychosis* <note>original Greek: "μετεμψυχώσει"; the doctrine of the transmigration of souls into different bodies, human or animal.</note>. For even if he had most fully admitted God, **Providence**, and the immortality of the mind, he would still not be one to persuade us that God performed miracles for his sake. For these precepts can be easily understood with a moderate amount of attention and meditation. But the following points will show that these genuine principles of **Natural Theology** <term>Natural Theology: the study of God based on reason and the observation of nature, rather than on divine revelation.</term> were disfigured by foolish opinions and worship. He ordered that God must be worshipped, but also **Demons** and **Heroes**. This life is so hemmed in by great pains and miseries that even the best of men, though they may have lived most peacefully and calmly, are nonetheless forced to admit that the pains they endured were greater than the pleasures they tasted. If, therefore, there is no hope in this life that we shall finally reach a harbor of tranquility, but instead must migrate through all eternity through innumerable bodies—animals and plants—then every effort toward living rightly is cast out from the soul. Surely, in that case, God would have created us for the purpose of doing evil and for eternal torment. **Pythagoras** himself, after he had inhabited many bodies (if it is right to believe such a thing), was ultimately treated poorly by the **Crotonians** <note>The inhabitants of Croton in southern Italy, where Pythagoras established his school; historical accounts suggest they eventually rose up against the Pythagorean sect.</note> and either ended his life in sorrow, or, as others claim, was handed over to the fire.

Finally, he taught that sacrifices must be made to Hercules on the eighth day of the beginning month, in consideration of his seven-month birth <note>Referring to the myth that Hercules was born after only seven months of gestation.</note>.

He further adds that one must not enter a temple except in pure clothing in which no one has slept: for sleep is a sign of sloth, just like the colors black and dark brown; but purity is a sign of evenness in reasoning and of justice. Moreover, he instructed that if blood is shed voluntarily in a temple, a purification must be performed either with gold or with the sea: since the former [gold] is the most beautiful of things and the measure of value by which all things are usually appraised; while the latter [the sea] is the primary offspring of moist nature and of the first and more common mat- <meta>This word is completed on the next page as "matter" (materiæ).</meta>

...here and there certain *ingenious and beautiful* precepts are brought forward by the Learned, but those have been torn away and abstracted from the body of the *entire Pythagorean Philosophy*, while meanwhile, countless *absurdities* and *old wives' tales* <note>original: "anilibus nugis" — a common Latin idiom for trivial or superstitious nonsense</note>, unworthy of a Philosopher, are wrapped in silence. Even if there were very many precepts consistent with reason and useful to the human race which had been put forward by Pythagoras without an admixture of error, this could clearly add no weight to demonstrating the certainty of miracles. For since among almost all Nations there have always been very many who, devoted to a more diligent cultivation of reason, followed the decrees of right reason, and yet were not famous for any miracles, a reason would have to be given why he especially should be adorned with this singular gift—he who brought forth nothing into the light except those things which can be learned by reason alone. But there is no need for us to subject this question to our examination. Those things already cited sufficiently testify (and I could bring forward many more if anyone requested it) that most of the *Decrees of Pythagoras* are obscure, absurd, superstitious, and contrary to the most pure worship and will of God.

*...from where Physicians are accustomed [to begin]. “For they too, by purging the stomachs, prevent some from being sick, and others they heal.”* <note>original Greek: και γαρ ἐκεινοι καθαιροντες τας γαστερας, τους μεν οὐδε νοσειν ἐωσι, τους δε ἰωνται</note>
*For these men, by purging the bellies, preserve some from disease and return others to health. It would have been better if **Apollonius** had begun his labors and studies by purging his brain. But it pleased **Apollonius** otherwise: hence he abstained from the eating of animals, as if it were impure and dulled the mind, but he ate delicacies and vegetables, saying that whatever the earth provided was pure. He affirmed that wine was indeed a pure drink, since it comes from a tree so gentle to men, but that it was contrary to a good state of mind, because it disturbs the **ether** <term>ether: in ancient physics, the "fifth element" or quintessence; here, it refers to the most refined, divine part of the human soul</term> which is in the soul. But it is no wonder that **Apollonius** knew these things; for, according to the testimony of **Philostratus**, he was on familiar terms with **Aesculapius** <note>The Greco-Roman god of medicine and healing; Apollonius was said to have lived in his temple at Aegae.</note>. He was initiated into that sacred Philosophy by a five-year silence, which nevertheless had a greater power over souls than the eloquence of the most silver-tongued Orators. **Philostratus** narrates the matter thus in chapter 15: Moreover, he spent this time of silence partly in **Pamphylia** and partly in **Cilicia** <note>Regions in what is now southern Turkey.</note>; and although he traveled through such soft and pampered nations, he never spoke, nor could he be led even to mutter. If ever he happened upon a rebellious city (and many were in discord for the sake of spectacles that possessed nothing praiseworthy), by stepping into the midst and showing himself openly, and indicating the rebuke he was preparing by his very hand and expression, he removed all confusion, so that everyone held their silence as if in the **mysteries** <note>Refers to the "Mystery Cults" of antiquity, such as the Eleusinian Mysteries, where initiates were bound by a sacred vow of secrecy and silence.</note>: so true is that saying of **Virgil**.* <note>The author alludes to a famous passage in Virgil's Aeneid (Book 1, lines 148–153), where a respected man silences a rioting crowd simply by his presence and authority.</note>

But **Apollonius** was not only a certain God, but also a King. For when a Satrap <note>term: *satrapa* — a provincial governor in the ancient Persian Empire.</note> of the **King of Babylon** asked who he was to enter the King’s borders, **Apollonius** replied: “The whole earth is mine; therefore, the power to travel wherever I please is granted to me.” Surely that saying of **Horace** is true:

> *Free, honored, beautiful, and finally, a King of Kings,*

However, although he claimed to be both God and King, he still displayed worship toward created things (page 39). When the King was about to sacrifice a white horse to the **Sun**, **Apollonius** approached and said: *“You, O King, may sacrifice in your own manner, but permit me to sacrifice according to my own rite.”* And taking incense in his hand, he said: *“O Sun, send me as far as I see fit across the lands; and grant that I may come into the acquaintance of good men; but as for the wicked, I wish neither to know them, nor to be known by them.”* Saying these things, he threw the incense into the fire, observing it closely to see in which part it rose, where it appeared dimmed, and how many sparks it emitted, and in what place; he was testing the fire to see if it appeared pure and capable of producing every good omen. Then he said, *“You, O King, may now proceed to perform your sacred rites according to your ancestral customs...”*

...as his ancestral rites allowed; and from there he withdrew from the sacrifice, lest he should enter into a communion of blood. I observe two things here. First is that **Apollonius** was devoted to the most absurd superstition. The ancients—whom **Homer** calls <term>thyoskopoi</term> <note>original Greek: *Θυοσκόπους*. Literally "smoke-watchers," these were diviners who interpreted the future by observing the flames and smoke of sacrificial offerings.</note>—diligently observed the movement of flame and smoke and took omens from them, which the late **Olearius** <note>Gottfried Olearius (1672–1715) was a German scholar and theologian who produced a famous edition of the works of Philostratus.</note> illustrates with many examples in his commentary on this passage.

Second: that this "Incomparable Man" approved of the worship of the Sun. Anyone can see how worthy such things are of a wise man and a philosopher sent from heaven—as he boasted himself to be. The wretched man was utterly ignorant of the nature of <term>rational worship</term> <note>original Greek: *λογικης λατρείας* (logikēs latreias). This is a biblical term from Romans 12:1, often translated as "spiritual service" or "reasonable worship," used here to contrast Christian reason with Apollonius's pagan rituals.</note>. 

However, our "King" was more successful in putting ghosts to flight than in rooting out idolatry, as **Philostratus** testifies in Book II, chapter 4. While they were making their journey (*so says the historian*), by the light of the bright moon, they encountered the ghost of an <term>Empusa</term> <note>In Greek folklore, an Empusa was a shape-shifting female demon or specter, often thought to be a sent by the goddess Hecate to devour travelers.</note>, now taking on one face, now another, and then completely vanishing. **Apollonius**, however, perceived what it was, and he himself attacked the **Empusa** with insults and urged his companions to do the same; for he said that this was the remedy against such an assault. And so the specter was driven away, shrieking, as ghosts are wont to do. Do you hear the voice of **Don Quixote**? <note>The author mockingly compares Apollonius's theatrical shouting at a "ghost" to the delusions of Miguel de Cervantes's famous knight, Don Quixote.</note>

There now follow certain lies that can almost be felt with the hand: I will say nothing now of what I mentioned above—that he claimed to have been at *Smyrna* and *Ephesus* at the same time. In Book III, chapter 23, he recounts that he was once the pilot of an *Egyptian* ship; in Book IV, chapter 11, he says he conversed with the dead; in chapter 16, he tells at length what kind of conversation he had with **Achilles**. He claims he obtained this through the use of prayers; he addressed **Achilles** thus: *"O Achilles, the common crowd of men thinks that you are indeed dead. I, however, by no means—"* <note>The text cuts off here, as the catchword "tiquam" indicates the next word on the following page will be "neutiquam," meaning "by no means" or "not at all."</note>

<meta>This page continues the critique of Apollonius of Tyana’s purported supernatural abilities. The previous page ended mid-sentence during a journey where Apollonius and his companions encountered a specter called an Empusa.</meta>

...before I yield to that opinion, nor does *Pythagoras* yield, the Father of my *Wisdom*. You, therefore, if we judge correctly, show us your form. For surely you will gain much benefit from my eyes, if you are permitted to use them as witnesses that you still live. After these things are narrated at great length, the historian <note>Referring to Philostratus, the primary biographer of Apollonius.</note> describes in what form he appeared and what he answered to the questions. Everyone can see that these are lies covered by more lies, lest the truth leak through. For this entire narrative was devised to add weight to the empty opinion concerning <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>original Greek: *μετεμψυχώσει*. The philosophical belief in the soul's migration into a new body after death, a core tenet of Pythagoreanism.</note>.

Since, however, *Apollonius* contends that he was trained in the art of summoning the dead, he is deservedly called a <term>sorcerer</term> <note>original Greek: *γοης* (goēs). In the ancient world, this term often carried a negative connotation of a charlatan or a "howler" who used lamentations to wake the dead.</note>. For as *Cedrenus* <note>Georgius Cedrenus, an 11th-century Byzantine historian who compiled various ancient sources.</note> testifies on page 41: "Sorcery is so named from the wailing and lamentations <note>original Greek: *γοων καὶ θρηνων* (goōn kai thrēnōn)</note> made around tombs by those who practice such things."

For this reason, even *Pythagoras* himself—the teacher of our subject—was marked with the same title by the *Phliasian* writer of the *Silli* <note>Timon of Phlius, a skeptical philosopher known for his "Silli," or satirical poems mocking other philosophers.</note>, as *Plutarch* testifies in his life of *Numa*, page 69:

> *Pythagoras, a sorcerer leaning toward opinions,*
> *who went hunting for men with the charm of his solemn speech:* **that is:**
> *Pythagoras the Magician, catching the aura of a name,*
> *And hunting the ears of men with grave discourses.*

*Philostratus* himself notes in Book 4, chapter 18, that this same title was given to *Apollonius* by the high priest of the Athenians. For when he wished to be initiated into the Athenian rites, the <term>Hierophant</term> <note>The chief priest at the Eleusinian Mysteries, who "showed the sacred things."</note> did not wish to grant him the sacred ceremonies, saying "he would never initiate a sorcerer, nor open Eleusis to a man not pure in matters of the divine."

We are certainly not unaware that *Philostratus* attempted to remove the title of *Enchanter* from *Apollonius* in Book 8, chapter 12. "Sorcerers," he says, "I consider to be the most wretched of men; some of them, resorting to the interrogation of phantoms, others to barbaric sacrifices, and others to chanting or anointing, claim to change the course of fate." And many...

i. e. *Enchanters (whom I judge to be the most wretched of all men) apply themselves partly to the tormenting of spirits, partly to barbarian sacrifices, and partly they boast that they can change the decrees of the fates with incantations or poisons; and many of them, when accused, have confessed that they were skilled in such arts. Apollonius, however, followed the decrees of the Fates, predicting only that those things would necessarily come to pass; he himself knew them beforehand, not by using incantations, but from those things which the gods showed him.*

But *Philostratus* struggles in vain: for my part, I would willingly believe that *Apollonius* did not enjoy a familiar association with demons, and was a mere <term>charlatan</term> <note>original Latin: *agyrtam*. A term for a wandering beggar-priest or a street performer who tricked the gullible.</note>; yet *Philostratus* himself speaks of him in such a way that men could not believe otherwise than that he was a <term>Mage</term> <note>original: *Magum*. In this historical context, a "Mage" refers to someone practicing "high" magic or sorcery, often viewed with suspicion by the authorities.</note> himself. From this, the Illustrious *Huetius* <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar who wrote the *Demonstratio Evangelica* (A Demonstration of the Gospel) to defend Christianity against philosophical critiques.</note> proves in his *Demonstration of the Gospel*, page 1067 of the Leipzig Edition, that there was a public rumor at that time, supported by other testimonies besides those we have already cited. He finally responds to this very objection of *Philostratus* just now brought forward, in this way: *Philostratus did not describe those signs (which are said to have been granted to him by the gods), nor could those things which he writes that Apollonius foreknew have been known in advance from the context of the events themselves. Furthermore, harmful and magical incantations can be pronounced in secret, even without the knowledge of those standing closest by. Then there are countless other types of secret divination accurately distinguished and noted by learned men, which Apollonius could have used.* And, after a few words: *Although because of these very things, if he is not quite convicted, we can certainly hold him suspect of this impiety; for from the ancient magic of these barbarian <term>Philosophers</term>...*

"Therefore," said **Apollonius**, "you would join yourself to her in marriage."

She told him to speak auspiciously <note>A common ancient phrase meaning "hush" or "don't tempt fate."</note>, and said to him, "Begone!" Pretending to be offended by what she heard, she railed against **philosophers** for a while, calling them perpetual triflers.

Secondly, Philostratus betrays his own bad faith; for who would believe that if the event had truly occurred in the heart of Greece, those circumstances would have remained unknown and been told to no one except Philostratus? Embellishments were needed to compose the story.

This is **Amasis**, the King of Egypt, from the district of **Sais**." <note>Amasis II was a real Pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty, known for his cleverness and building projects</note> When the lion heard this, he let out a miserable roar and a lament; kneeling down, he wailed and even shed tears. Stroking him, **Apollonius** said, "I judge that the lion should be sent to **Leontopolis** <note>literally "City of the Lion," an ancient Egyptian city where lions were treated as sacred</note> and placed there in the temple. For I judge it unworthy for a King, though turned into a beast more royal than all others, to wander about just as beggars are accustomed to do." 

Thus, **Apollonius** not only lies splendidly when he claims it was revealed to him which soul occupied that lion, but he also confirmed the **Egyptians** as the authors of **reincarnation**. Indeed...

# CHAPTER VII.

## On the Character, Morals, and Doctrine
## of Francis of Assisi.

We have so far described the habits and teaching of Pythagoras and Apollonius. It is time, therefore, for us to place before the reader's eyes the lives and precepts of others who are said to have been famous for miracles, so that it may be judged by what right we may assign them, in what follows, to the same class as those previously mentioned. And first, let *Francis of Assisi* <note>The founder of the Franciscan Order (1181–1226), known for his poverty and reported miracles</note> step onto the stage and testify to the role he played. Let us *hear* first from *Bonaventure* <note>Saint Bonaventure, a major medieval theologian who wrote the official biography of Francis</note>, and then from the *Alcoran of the Franciscans* <note>original: "Alcoranum Franciscanorum" — a polemical title for a book detailing the life of Francis, mockingly comparing Franciscan rules to the Quran</note> and the antiquities, books we mentioned earlier. 

Certainly, the things we said about the habits and teaching of *Pythagoras* and *Apollonius*, however absurd they may be, are light and tolerable when compared with the *sayings and deeds of Francis* and the others. What happened to the *Illustrious Huet* <note>Pierre-Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and famous scholar</note> as a boy reading the life of Apollonius, happened to me while leafing through the Biography <note>original Greek: Βιογραφίαν</note> written by Bonaventure. It tells (so says *Huet*) *so many fables, so many dreams, of such little wit and such little flavor, that when I read them, I was immediately seized by satiety and disgust, and I seemed to hear a wet-nurse talking about the towers of Lamia <note>A child-eating monster from Greek myth</note> and the combs of the sun to soothe her puppet to sleep.* 

But lest anyone think I am making false accusations, I will bring forward so many examples of madness, superstition, absurdities, and even blasphemies which shine forth from *Francis’s* life, character, and precepts, that no one could ask for more.

<summary>The author begins a new chapter critiquing the life of St. Francis of Assisi, arguing that his legendary miracles and hagiography are even more ridiculous and superstitious than those of ancient pagan philosophers.</summary>
<keywords>Francis of Assisi, Saint Bonaventure, Alcoran of the Franciscans, Pierre-Daniel Huet, hagiography, superstition, miracles, religious polemic</keywords>

--- Page 167 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous page, the author begins a detailed critique of the life of Saint Francis of Assisi as recorded by his biographer, Saint Bonaventure. The previous page ended with the author describing his own reaction to reading these "fables," which he found as lacking in substance as the pagan legends of Apollonius.</meta>

I will follow Bonaventure himself: on page 4, Bonaventure relates by what path Francis arrived at seeing such great light, by which he was illuminated throughout his whole life. When he had given his own garments to a soldier (so says the **biographer** <note>original Greek: βιογράφος, referring here to Saint Bonaventure</note>), and when on the following night he had given himself over to sleep, divine mercy showed him a large and spacious palace filled with military arms, marked with the sign of the Cross of Christ. This was shown so that it might demonstrate beforehand that the mercy shown to the poor soldier for the love of the Supreme King was to be compensated with an incomparable reward. From this, when he asked whose things all these were, it was answered by a heavenly assertion that they would belong to him and his soldiers. 

Awakening therefore in the morning, since he did not yet have a mind trained in scrutinizing divine mysteries, and did not know how to pass through the forms of visible things to the contemplation of the truth of invisible things, he estimated the unusual vision to be a sign of great prosperity. Therefore, since the good man did not understand the meaning of this vision, he traveled to **Apulia** <note>A region in Southern Italy</note>, intending to enlist in military service. But while he was on the journey, he heard the Lord saying to him at night in a familiar address: 

*“Francis, who can do more for you, the Lord or the servant? The rich man or the poor man?”* 

When Francis answered Him that both the Lord and the rich man could do more, the Lord immediately replied: 

*“Why then do you leave the Lord for the servant, and the wealthy God for a poor man?”* 

And Francis said, *“Lord, what do you want me to do?”* and the Lord said to him: *“Return to your own land, because the vision you saw prefigures a spiritual effect, to be fulfilled in you not by human, but by divine arrangement.”* 

He returned, therefore, to **Assisi**; but he did not yet understand the vision. A miracle then followed, to be confirmed at last by a fourth vision, in Section 5. In the age of *Francis*, the power given to the Demon was greater than in ours. Now, having become kinder toward mortals, he can allow them to take their sleep in those very beds, filled with feathers and softly spread. A **Swallow**, commanded to be silent in the name of **Francis**, kept a deep silence. Furthermore (page 94), the **Little Boat** which he boarded moved away from the land of its own accord. I shall add one more example—for I am weary of these absurdities <note>original: *tædet ineptiarum*</note>—which appears on page 92.

### ❦ ) 113 ( ❦

When he approached Bevagna <note>original: *Bevanio*</note>, he came to a certain place where a vast multitude of birds of various kinds had gathered. When the **Saint of God** saw them, he ran eagerly to the spot and greeted them as if they were rational participants in thought. While everyone else watched, the birds turned toward him; even those in the bushes bowed their heads as he approached, gazing at him in an unusual manner. He went right up to them and earnestly urged them all to hear the **Word of God**, saying:

> My brother birds, you owe much praise to your Creator, who clothed you in feathers and gave you wings for flying, granted you the purity of the air, and governs you without any worry on your part.

When he spoke these and similar things to them, the little birds, acting in a wonderful manner, began to stretch out their necks, extend their wings, open their beaks, and look at him attentively. He himself, with a marvelous fervor of Spirit, passed through the middle of them, his tunic touching them; yet not one of them moved from its place until the sign of the Cross was made and permission was given. With the blessing of the **Man of God**, they all flew away together. **Bonaventure** <note>Saint Bonaventure (1221–1274), the Franciscan theologian and official biographer of St. Francis</note> would not have done badly if he had added to all this the saying of **Phaedrus** <note>A 1st-century Roman writer famous for his poetic fables</note>, who said:

> *If anyone should wish to slander me*
> *Because trees speak, and not only beasts,*
> *Let him remember that we are merely jesting with fictional fables.* <note>original: *Calumniari si quis autem voluerit, / Quod arbores loquantur non tantum feræ / Fictis jocari nos meminerit fabulis.*</note>

But one expects such honesty in vain from a foolish and inept Monk. For my part, that passage from **Lucian** <note>Lucian of Samosata, a 2nd-century Greek satirist who mocked religious charlatans and superstitions</note> in *The Lover of Lies* <note>original: *Philopseude*</note> comes to mind again and again. For when **Philocles** had narrated countless wonders and splendid lies, he said to **Tychiades**: "If you had seen these things, you would no longer doubt." To which the latter replied:

...he invented the prayer formulas *Hail Holy Queen* <note>original: *Salve Regina*</note> and the *Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarium*</note>, something which any superstitious person could have done, but no one with a sound mind. Hence, in this very biography <note>original Greek: βιογραφια (*biographia*)</note> no argument exists (nor certainly can any be brought forward) to prove that it was necessary for others, having established a certain society, to follow the same insanity after the example of this fanatic man. For if new societies had to be established every time a dull-witted person decided to act foolishly and distinguish himself from the rest of the crowd by his voice, diet, or clothing, the world itself could never contain the madhouses <note>original: *gyrgathos*, likely a reference to cages or asylums for the deranged.</note>.

Everyone knows, even if I remain silent, how much harm the <term>Orders of Monks and Nuns</term> <note>These refer to the various religious communities, such as the Dominicans or Franciscans, who lived under specific monastic rules.</note> have brought upon our most pure Religion and the Commonwealths. These sleek Monks, with their well-groomed skin, should be driven out of the cloisters with whips and forced either to devote themselves to the liberal arts and disciplines or to serve the interests of the Fatherland. But about these matters, it is better to remain silent than to speak insufficiently. 

However, lest anyone misinterpret my words, I must add that when I mention *Monks*, I do not mean those *learned men* who have served the *cause of letters* <note>original: *re literaria*</note> so well, of whom I am well aware there is no small number, especially in *France* <note>original: *Gallia*</note>. I am speaking of those who, under the guise of piety, pursue a fat leisure and pamper their skin, neglecting all the duties they could perform for *God* and *human society*. I say only this: in this biography <note>original Greek: βιογραφια (*biographia*)</note>, visions are appealed to as the most certain proof for establishing a new Society.

The Pope's Council laments those who died in innocence; we do not yet know what the Lord Pope has written back in response to this, except that he regrets enough that he permitted such great power to the said Master Conrad, from which such confusion emerged. Furthermore, there is a certain new vision in Germany, by which it is conjectured that the same Master Conrad is damned.* Thus far Alberic <note>Alberic of Trois-Fontaines, a Cistercian chronicler whose work is the source for this account.</note>.

Having been wonderfully refreshed by this sight, *Ignatius* suddenly conceived such weariness and disgust for those things which are considered primary among blind mortals—and especially those things joined with dishonorable pleasure—that the vision immediately wiped from the man’s memory all images of such things, however much they had been strengthened by long use and old age. It is so true that those who act imprudently are those who demand that great geniuses conform to the common rules of prudence; how necessary it is that this be observed will become clear through the introduction of other examples. ***Ignatius***, having returned from the Holy Land and stayed for a short time in Italy, hurried to ***Spain***, his homeland. At that time, however, a serious war <note>Likely the Italian War of 1521–1526 between the Habsburg Emperor Charles V and King Francis I of France.</note> was raging between ***Christian Kings***, and the roads were dangerous with killings and robberies. ***Ignatius*** was therefore warned to turn aside from the main road. 

*But he (these are the words of Maffei <note>Giovanni Pietro Maffei, a Jesuit historian and author of a famous life of Ignatius.</note>), whom an ardent hatred of self and a love of imitating the patience of Christ rendered fearless, nevertheless continued to go straight. Soon, however, he was taken for a spy by soldiers, captured, and exposed to mockery.* 

If anyone were to judge this matter according to common sense, they would judge that ***Ignatius*** had suffered a punishment worthy of his own folly. But they would judge poorly. For while he was suffering these things, *a certain vision was presented to him of Christ the Lord (as Maffei tells it) as he was sent by Pilate through the middle of the city to the tribunals of Herod, despised and mocked by him through the greatest injury and indignity, and with the entire populace laughing and hissing, led before the eyes of men once and again: Ignatius marveled and rejoiced that he had been made, in some small way, a participant in this disgrace.*

<meta>This page continues the account of Ignatius of Loyola’s education in Barcelona. ...ready and agile in practice; if the word "love," or any other such word, reminded him of those things which he was accustomed to piously and religiously contemplate and reflect upon, he would suddenly be almost **drawn away from his senses**, his whole mind being snatched into a **contemplation of divine charity** and eternal bliss. 

The result of this was not only that he could commit nothing new to his memory, but even that if anything had been previously impressed there, it was immediately erased by the rush of new and more excellent images. The **crafty enemy of the human race** <note>A traditional epithet for the Devil.</note>, as if foreseeing what was to come, even helped this along on his part, offering him frequent lights of understanding at that very time and opening up the hidden **mysteries of Holy Scripture**. 

When he saw this, and after he had often tried in vain to restrain this wandering of the mind, he easily perceived—through that **discernment of spirits** <term>discernment of spirits: a key Jesuit concept involving the practice of determining whether a spiritual impulse or "light" comes from God, from one's own ego, or from a deceptive source</term> which he had developed through long practice—the fraud of the Devil trying to call him away from the **study of Letters**. Since he desired to achieve the very purpose for which he had come to **Barcelona** <note>original: "Barcinonem"</note> through labor and diligence, he devised this plan to drive away that nuisance. 

There was a church of the **Blessed Virgin**, known as **"of the Sea"** <note>The Basilica of Santa Maria del Mar in Barcelona, located near the medieval schools.</note>, which was close to the school <note>original: "gymnasio"</note>. In that church, after having offered the proper prayers to God and the Virgin, he called for **Ardévol** <note>Jerónimo Ardévol, the grammar master who taught the adult Ignatius the basics of Latin alongside young children.</note> on the basis of their friendship and explained the whole situation to him just as it was. Then he threw himself at the man's feet, begging him again and again not to give up on the undertaking. He promised that, as long as he did not lack bread and water, he would attend the classes regularly for the next two years, and even longer if necessary, and would diligently apply himself to his studies. He begged and asked that Ardévol demand a daily lesson from him no less than from the others, and that if he were idle, he should treat him just like any other boy in the flock, according to his own judgment, with both harsh words and **blows** <note>Flogging or corporal punishment was the standard method of discipline in 16th-century schools, even for a student of Ignatius's age and social standing.</note>.

Meanwhile, as he was wonderfully eager to learn and searching for all shortcuts to study, some suggested to him—in order to join piety with more elegant learning—that he should studiously read through the **Enchiridion of a Christian Soldier** <note>A famous work of humanist spirituality by Erasmus of Rotterdam.</note> by **Erasmus of Rotterdam**, who was considered a suitable **Master of Latinity** in those days. 

When he had begun to do this, he quickly felt that by this reading the fervor of the **Spirit** in him was being extinguished, as if cold water had been poured over it. Having consulted **God** through prayer, he cast that book aside in such a way that he never took it into his hands again; and much later, having been created **General** <note>The Superior General, the head of the Jesuit Order.</note>, he forbade all the works of that writer to be read in the **Society of Jesus**; not because he thought every single thing was infected with heretical poison, but lest anyone, perhaps captivated by the man's wit and sharp tongue, should gradually descend, as often happens, from the incorrupt to the corrupt.

A Bavarian Jesuit <note>original: "suita Bavarus," likely a contraction of "Jesuita Bavarus," referring to Jeremias Drexel (1581–1638), who famously argued that Latin was the language spoken in heaven.</note> contends that the blessed in heaven will speak Latin; therefore, it had to be striven for that **Ignatius** be drawn away from the love of this language, lest perhaps he practice on earth those things of which the knowledge persists in heaven. Perhaps the **Devil** did this without a bad intention. He seems to have foreseen that the disciples of **Ignatius** would preside over Schools and Gymnasiums <note>secondary schools</note>, and would carefully instill the precepts of the humanities but would often neglect weightier studies, and would deceive many with the instrument of this language. In this, however, the **Devil**—if he had obtained what he wanted—would have looked out for himself very poorly; but only the **Devil** knows the true cause.

Secondly, since the **Devil** had thrust wonderful visions upon **Ignatius** to call him away from the study of the Latin language—nay, what you might wonder at, for that purpose he revealed the hidden *Mysteries* of **Holy Scripture**—while God, consulted through prayer, likewise deterred him from reading the book of **Erasmus**, it is most clearly and most evidently apparent that **Ignatius** was hardly able to distinguish divine inspiration (if any ever happened to him) from diabolical suggestions. 

For if the **Devil** as well as God can instill hidden **Mysteries**, and indeed those of the **Holy Scripture**, into the mind of a man, there is no reasoning by which divine operations can be distinguished from the suggestions of an infernal spirit. No one doubts that this power should be attributed to God; according to **Ignatius**, however, the **Devil** can do the same. Therefore **Ignatius** did not know whether all those visions in which he perceived the most **holy** things were from the **Devil** or not.

...example <note>original: "plum", completing "Exemplum" from the previous page</note> of the **Most Holy Father, Ignatius**, his disciples thought should not only be imitated but also extended to other things. How pure is the pleasure one tastes when, on such an occasion, we share with one another everything we think and everything we feel in the depths of our hearts!”*

They were debating her **virginity**; and while that wicked man <note>The "wicked man" refers to a Moor Ignatius met on the road, as recounted in traditional biographies of the saint.</note> admitted that she had indeed been chaste and untouched before the birth, he claimed this was by no means the case after the birth. **Ignatius**, on the other hand, strove to call the man back from such an error by whatever arguments he could. *zeal for **penitence** <note>original: "pænitentiæ"</note> among the needy and the filthy, he began the life which we shall now describe. He begged for his daily sustenance from door to door with the most humble prayers; he fasted the entire week, except for the Lord’s Day; in his simple meals, he was content with plain bread, and when thirst pressed him, he drank from running water. He began to leave his hair uncombed and filthy, and even allowed his nails to grow long through prolonged neglect; and in this so harsh and so horrid a way of life, he constantly shunned everything that could bring any delight or relief to his afflicted flesh.* 

*On another occasion, when he had recovered from an illness, he condemned this way of life; he forbade (so says Maffei <note>Giovanni Pietro Maffei (1533–1603), a Jesuit priest and biographer of Ignatius</note>, page 31) the body to be defrauded of due sleep and food, having been taught by many experiences at that time that just as the soul is invigorated by moderate sobriety, so by immoderate wakefulness or starvation the strengths are so broken and weakened that the mind, deprived of their service, can hardly perform its duty or rise to the contemplation of divine things.*

Certainly, this action of Ignatius was not only plainly stupid, but also set a very bad example; for those insults brought upon him because of the filth and novelty of his garments, not only [contribute] nothing to religious [scruples]...

[...joy] do you see? Go on then, go on and fulfill that wicked lust. I shall torment myself here for your sake for as long as it takes, until I turn away the heavenly wrath from you by my own suffering.

On page 170: for the salvation of his pupil, he abstained from all food and drink for three whole days. On page 171: when he had gone to visit a certain man suffering from a severe and contagious ulcer, and had repeatedly touched him while he lay there for the sake of ministering to him, a fear came over **Ignatius** upon his departure that he might have contracted the plague from that contact with his right hand. When this suspicion began to trouble the man quite vehemently, and threatened to call him away from such <term>works of charity</term> <note>original: "caritatis officio"</note> in the future, he immediately burned with indignation against himself, recognizing the trick <note>A common theme in Jesuit hagiography where the "enemy of human nature" (the devil) uses natural fear to discourage holy work.</note>. He repeatedly thrust his right hand into his mouth and rebuked himself of his own accord: "You who are so anxious about one hand, what will you do for the whole body?" By this act of fortitude, he both drove away his present fear and proved himself vigorous and cheerful in continuing to perform the same works of piety.

In **Paris** (page 173), he was invited in jest by a certain nobleman to see if he wished to play <term>billiards</term> <note>original: "trudiculis" – a game played on an oblong table where ivory balls were struck through a narrow arch, a precursor to modern billiards.</note>. "I will indeed play," said **Ignatius**. "But with what wager," the other replied, "since you have no money?" Then **Ignatius** answered: "With this wager: that I shall serve you for a certain number of days, by your choice if you win; but by mine, if I emerge the victor." 

When that condition was accepted, they indeed entered into the contest. To judge correctly, the faculty of thinking in other men is called **reason** <note>original: "ratio"</note>; and the standard, or the principles of **right reason**, or the **will of God**—whether natural or revealed—according to which people are accustomed to judge their own actions, are clearly different.

A man of this kind—one who is free from superstition but convinced of the primary tenets of *Natural Religion* <term>Natural Religion: A system of belief popular in the 17th and 18th centuries that argued God's existence and moral laws could be discovered through human reason and observing nature, without needing supernatural revelation.</term>—cannot, without wounding his conscience, cast a vote of approval <note>original: "album calculum adjicere"; literally "to add a white pebble," a classical metaphor for giving a favorable judgment or acquittal in a trial.</note> for the arguments of a *Missionary*, even if that missionary sprinkles certain dogmas of the Christian religion into his decrees. ### CHAPTER XI.

->*The miracles of Pythagoras, Apollonius, Francis, etc., are not from God, because they subvert the truth and divinity of the Christian Religion.*<-

Among the blessings of the current century in which we live, I count the fact that the *Truth* and *Divinity* of the Christian Religion has not only been proven and established by most excellent men endowed with the highest genius using the most solid reasons, but has also been *most strongly defended* against all the objections of unbelievers. It is not my task to protect this same truth, already so excellently demonstrated, by a tedious repetition of the arguments by which the <term>Ministers of the Word of God</term> <note>original: "V. D.", likely abbreviating *Verbi Dei Ministri*.</note> are accustomed to prove it. Regarding miracles, there has been intense dispute on more than one occasion; yet all who believe that miracles occur confess that God does not use miracles except to confirm the most holy and divine matters. Nor will I now investigate whether those miracles said to have been performed in the first centuries after the departure of Christ were truly carried out. I admit that God—after He once confirmed the divinity of the Christian Religion with miracles—can confirm His decrees with miracles as the occasion arises; though I do not see a reason why God, after He has sufficiently and more than enough provided for humanity in this regard, ought to perform the same thing again and again. Whatever <note>original: "quid autem", continuing from the previous page's "What-".</note> the case may be regarding that, this much is certain to me and I am convinced: that God is not accustomed to performing miracles to prove lies, but rather to confirm the most holy doctrine. The <term>dogmas</term> <note>established religious doctrines</note> which *Christ* and the *Apostles* taught were either of the sort that can be known by reason alone—such as that God is the Best, Wisest, Freest, and Holiest, the Creator and Preserver of the whole human race and of all things; that the mind was created by God and is subject to certain laws intended for the salvation of each and every person, and is thus capable of punishment and reward, and is, finally, immortal and destined to endure eternally—or they were Decrees which become known only through the *Revelation* of God. Specifically, these concern the origin of sin, the corruption of the human race, the *Messiah*, His person, offices, works, the administration of the whole work of grace, and so on. 

As far as the former <note>the rational truths</note> are concerned, they are not only delivered and emphasized clearly everywhere, but they are also proposed with such great evidence that, in the opinion of *Philosophers* and *Theologians*, they wonderfully confirm the decrees of reason. In October, on the Feast of St. Francis, founder of the Order of the Barefoot Friars <note>A common name for the Franciscans due to their vow of poverty and practice of wearing sandals or going barefoot</note>, which falls on the 4th of this month, one obtains indulgences as on New Year’s Day in January; additionally, Alexander IV grants 40 years; John XXII, 10 years and 50 days; Sixtus IV, one hundred years and as many quadragenas.
