Again, John XXII granted for every day within the octave <note>The "octave" is the eight-day period of celebration following a major church feast</note> an indulgence of 100 years and 50 days. Sixtus V grants a plenary indulgence <note>A "plenary" or full indulgence is believed to remove all temporal punishment due for sins</note>. In the calendar for the Confraternity of the Holy Rosary of Jesus and Mary, it states on the 4th of August, on the Feast of Dominic <note>Saint Dominic, founder of the Dominican Order</note>, a full indulgence. See the same, page 419.

*Men are never commanded to arrange their lives according to the standard of divine Revelation, nor to look to it as a rich treasury for their future needs. Instead, visions and absurd decrees are the standards for our actions: in life, death, and adversities, people are saved by imploring the help of this or that saint—for example, Francis, Dominic, etc.—rather than the help of God. Let one read the examples of those who were saved by the help of Loyola <note>Ignatius of Loyola, the founder of the Jesuit Order</note>, Francis, and others, and it will be clear that such power is attributed to their merits—indeed, to their garments and various parts of their bodies—which Holy Scripture is accustomed to attribute solely to the divine passions of Christ.*

<summary>This page details the specific, often lengthy indulgences granted by various popes for the feast days of Saint Francis and Saint Dominic, followed by a Protestant polemical critique arguing that such devotions replace the authority of Scripture and the merits of Christ with "absurd" saint-worship.</summary>

What shall I say about *Transubstantiation* <term>Transubstantiation: the Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the actual body and blood of Christ</term>, a dogma of all those ever devised by the folly of human wit, the most absurd and most ridiculous? ...they were [more] than *truth* would allow; they would attribute to *Christ* alone those things which also belong to *Dominic*, *Francis*, and *Loyola* <note>Referring to the founders of the three major orders: St. Dominic (Dominicans), St. Francis of Assisi (Franciscans), and Ignatius of Loyola (Jesuits).</note>; but who in the future will be able to have faith in the *Legates of Christ* regarding the other things they tell, if in those matters which comprise the heart of the issue, they have shamefully deceived us? To believe, moreover, that *God* performed miracles to confirm the doctrine of each individual <note>That is, to confirm the specific, often conflicting, theological positions of different Catholic orders.</note> would be the same as asserting that *God* wills contrary things—and wills them seriously—which is the same as doing away with *God* altogether. 

Let us proceed from *Dogmas* to the precepts of *Christ* and the *Apostles*, and their life and character: let us compare these with the precepts of those *Monks*, their life, and their whole way of living. The precepts of *Christ* are most agreeable to reason, and are *most useful, most holy, and most just* for the whole human race and all its members. They are derived partly from the *laws of right reason*, and partly from the character and nature of the Religion inculcated *by Christ and the Apostles*. These are precepts the summary of which is the *Love of God and neighbor*. 

*Holy Scripture* leads us to the observance of these precepts with the weightiest arguments; drawn from *God’s Example*, His *Goodness*, *Mercy*, and the *Dominion* He holds over *His Creatures*, and from the *excellence of the things themselves*: the same *Most Holy God* promises that He will be present with His favor and help to those who wish to order their mind and life according to the standard of *most holy discipline*. In a word, these precepts of the *Gospel* are so excellent that even the *Deists* <note>Thinkers who believe in a creator God based on reason but reject supernatural revelation or organized religion.</note>, for whom the *Mysteries and dogmas of the Christian Religion* are repulsive, praise and admire them.

# CHAPTER XIII.

## *An inquiry into whether those Miracles should be attributed to the Devil.*

I believe we have sufficiently proven that those miracles, for which **Pythagoras**, **Francis**, and the others are said to have been *Illustrious*, can have neither *God* as their *Author*, nor a *good Angel*. It remains, therefore, that we inquire to whom at last these Miracles are to be attributed. One of two things must be chosen: namely, we must say either that the *Devil* is the *Author* of those miracles; or that they are entirely false and fabricated by unscrupulous men <note>original: "maleferiatis hominibus"—literally "men keeping holiday badly," a Latin idiom for idle or mischievous people who use their leisure for deception.</note>. Among those who think that *God*, no less than *good and evil Angels*, can perform miracles, most concede to the opinion that those miracles produced by **Pythagoras** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher (c. 570–495 BC) to whom many supernatural abilities, such as bilocation and talking to animals, were attributed in later biographies.</note> and the others cannot arise from any cause other than the *Devil*, the most bitter and cunning enemy of the *Human Race*. And no small reasons seem to be able to be brought forward to defend this opinion.

First, indeed, the very nature of the matter seems to add strength to this view. Truly, the *Decrees* of these men are so adverse to reason, so childish, and so contrary to the *Majesty of the Divine* <note>original: "Numinis Majestati"</note>; their worship is so inept, ridiculous, and monstrous, that it can hardly be imagined that any other cause exists for such shameless superstition. I will not repeat what I have already said above regarding the superstition introduced by **Pythagoras** and **Apollonius** <note>Apollonius of Tyana (c. 15–100 AD), a Greek Neopythagorean philosopher whose life was often compared to that of Jesus in antiquity to challenge Christian claims.</note>, how foul it is and contrary to proper worship; I will say this one thing about the *Religion* and worship of **Francis** <note>Saint Francis of Assisi (1181–1226).</note>, etc., if—

## CHAPTER XIV.

->*The miracles attributed to Pythagoras, Apollonius, Francis, Dominic, and Loyola were fabricated by credulous and idle men.*<-

---

In the preceding chapters, we have proved that the miracles attributed to Pythagoras and the others have neither God nor the Devil as their author. It remains, therefore, for us to show that those events never happened, but were devised by credulous and idle <note>original: maleferiatis—literally "badly holidayed," referring to people who use their leisure time for mischief or foolishness</note> men, and then later amplified by those who followed. We warn in advance, however, that while we say those miracles were fabricated, we do not deny that those very men to whom such things are ascribed—through their foolish actions and a certain sought-after excellence above other men—were to a greater or lesser degree the instigators <note>literally "authors"</note> of such stories being spread among the common people <note>original: Vulgus</note>, partly by the credulous and partly by the idle. I have warned more than once in the preceding sections that all of them, though distinguished by varying degrees of folly and malice, spoke and ordered their lives and habits in such a way that they were little different from fools <note>original: morionibus</note> and fanatics. Come then, let us begin with Pythagoras, to see upon what witnesses the opinion regarding the miracles performed by him rests: Among those who claim that the Samian philosopher <note>Pythagoras of Samos.</note> was made illustrious by so many miracles, Iamblichus and Porphyrius <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who wrote biographies of Pythagoras centuries after his death, filled with supernatural tales.</note> must be mentioned.

<summary>The author begins Chapter XIV by arguing that the miracles associated with both ancient philosophers and Catholic saints are human fabrications rather than supernatural events. He contends that these figures behaved eccentrically to encourage such myths, which were then recorded by unreliable biographers.</summary>

<keywords>Pythagoras, Apollonius of Tyana, St. Francis of Assisi, St. Dominic, Ignatius of Loyola, skepticism, miracles, hagiography, Iamblichus, Porphyry</keywords>

--- Page 382 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page regarding the lack of credible witnesses for the miracles of Pythagoras. The previous page ended by asking upon what witnesses the stories of the Samian philosopher (Pythagoras) rest.</meta>

<page-num>294</page-num>
<meta>catchword: for</meta>

He who narrates a history or a past event either saw it himself or received it from *trustworthy* men who lived at the time the event is said to have occurred. We do not admit uncertain traditions, rumors, or "fame"—that messenger of both truth and falsehood—as indubitable histories. Moreover, it is necessary that the person who narrates a thing they have seen or heard be an upright man, *free from love, hatred, and anger*. For if the most serious reasons exist that could induce him to narrate the matter poorly <note>In this context, "poorly" (malè) refers to a biased or inaccurate account influenced by personal feelings.</note>, we do not easily admit his testimony.

However, the era of *Porphyry* and *Iamblichus* <note>Neoplatonist philosophers writing in the 3rd and 4th centuries AD, long after Pythagoras's death in the 5th century BC.</note> occurred in the third and fourth centuries after the birth of Christ. But *Pythagoras*, according to *Dodwell*, lived in the 52nd Olympiad; according to *Lloyd* and *Bentley* <note>Henry Dodwell, William Lloyd, and Richard Bentley were prominent 17th and 18th-century scholars of chronology and classical history.</note>, he lived in the forty-third. Since, therefore, those two writers lived so many centuries after *Pythagoras*, it is necessary for them to call upon ancient and sufficiently trustworthy witnesses when they wish to persuade us that those miracles were truly performed.

Yet *Iamblichus* and *Porphyry*, in the passages cited above where they begin their narration of reported miracles, appeal to no witness at all who saw them. instead, they narrate as if *from a tripod* <note>original: ex tripode; an idiom referring to the Oracle of Delphi, meaning to speak with absolute authority but without providing evidence or logic.</note>, believing that the matter should not be investigated further. At the start of his work, *Iamblichus* reveals enough about the foundations upon which his *Biography* <term>Greek: Biographia (Βιογραφία) — a written account of a life.</term> is built: *Nor*, he says, *will it cause us hesitation that this Sect has long lain neglected; for it is wrapped in foreign teachings and certain secret symbols; and because it is also obscured by forged and counterfeit writings, and hedged in by many other difficulties of that kind...*

<summary>The author critiques the historical reliability of Iamblichus and Porphyry, arguing that they lived centuries after Pythagoras and failed to cite contemporary witnesses for the miracles they attributed to him. He dismisses their accounts as being based on biased traditions and "counterfeit writings" rather than solid evidence.</summary>

Regarding the story that Pythagoras showed his golden thigh to Abaris, <note>Abaris the Hyperborean was a legendary sage and priest of Apollo; the "golden thigh" was a famous claim intended to prove Pythagoras's divinity or status as a reincarnation of Apollo.</note> he says it is "widely celebrated." <note>original Greek: πάνυ τεθρύλληται</note> To be sure, Plutarch, Diogenes Laertius, and Aelian—all writers born so many centuries after Pythagoras—recount that fable; therefore, the matter is "worthy of all acceptance." <note>original Greek: πάσης ἀποδοχῆς ἀξία</note> We shall soon see about the testimonies of the cited authors. 1. That no written records survive, either by *Pythagoras* or from any other trustworthy witness.
2. That there were many men named *Pythagoras* <note>A common historical argument used to explain the wildly contradictory accounts of his life by suggesting different individuals were confused into one.</note>.

4. That all testimonies are of a much later age.
5. That many signs of **Imposture** are detected in the actions of *Pythagoras*.
6. That the symbolic <note>original: "Emblematicam"</note> method of philosophizing gave rise to many foolish fables, and
7. From this, in my opinion, it is easy to guess how the reputation for the wonders performed by *Pythagoras* arose.

Thus says the most learned **Huet**: if anyone is so shameless as to sell such things as truth, does he deserve credit in anything else? He who has once crossed the boundaries of modesty must be thoroughly and actively shameless. **Philostratus** did this with all his effort. The countless fables cited so far from **Huet** are not enough, but miracles and portents must be added so that nothing is missing; we have brought forward a part of them above. <meta>This page continues the critique of Damis’s reliability as a witness to the life of Apollonius of Tyana. Having previously established Damis as a simpleton, the author now examines specific instances where Damis claims to have witnessed divine behavior or provides historically questionable descriptions.</meta>

He reports concerning **Damis**: he says indeed: *“Then for the first time **Damis** perceived the nature of **Apollonius** more accurately, that it was divine and greater than human. For while performing no sacred rites (for how could he have in prison?), nor using prayers, nor uttering any word, he held the shackles <note>original: *pedicas*</note> in contempt; and again, having inserted his leg into them, he conducted himself as if he were bound by chains.”* Having brought these things forward, **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a Christian polemicist who wrote a famous critique of Philostratus’s biography of Apollonius.</note>, laughing (page 450), adds that **Philostratus** and **Damis** say these things falsely. 

I, however, would not want to find fault with the disciple for his slowness <note>Referring to the "slowness of mind" or stupidity attributed to Damis on the previous page.</note>, in that, despite spending his whole life with him and seeing him perform wonders through the intervention of certain superstitious rites, he thought him to excel nothing in mortal nature; but indeed, even after such a great work had been performed, he remains ignorant of what kind of person he truly is. And as is natural for one who is ignorant, he is distressed for him and fears, just as if he were a defenseless <note>original: *nudus*, literally "naked" or "unprotected."</note> man, lest anything happen to him that he would least desire. 

While I make mention of **Babylon**, it must be noted at the same time that **Damis** is guilty of an open lie; for in Chapter 21, Book I, he narrates what was done in **Babylon**. And he describes the magnificence and splendor of that city in such a way that you would believe **Babylon** had not yet been desolated <note>By the 1st century AD, contemporary Roman historians reported that Babylon was largely a ruin, contradicting Damis's description of a thriving metropolis.</note> in that age, contrary to what **Pliny**, **Pausanias**, and **Tacitus** testify; regarding this matter, one should consult **Bochart** in *Canaan*, Book 4, Chapter 15. **Olearius** <note>Gottfried Olearius (1672–1715), a scholar known for his edition of Philostratus.</note> accuses him timidly enough, but the famous **Brucker** <note>Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770), a pioneering historian of philosophy.</note> openly and simply accuses him of an impudent lie (page 240, *History of Philosophy*, Volume 3). In Book II of the *Life of Apollonius*, Chapter 13, page 51, **Damis** tells many mythical <note>original: *fabulosa*</note> tales about the **Caucasus**, namely that **Prometheus** <note>The Titan from Greek mythology who was chained to a rock in the Caucasus as punishment for giving fire to humanity.</note> had been bound upon it, etc. **Philostratus** adds: *“and **Damis** says that chains were fastened to the rocks, which it is not easy to understand the...”* <note>original Greek: *καὶ δεσμὰ ὁ Δαμις ἀνῆφθαι τῶν πετρῶν λέγει, οὐ ῥᾴδιον ξυμβαλλειν τὴν*</note>

"For," he says, "one should not pay attention to **Moeragenes**, who, though he composed four books on **Apollonius**, was ignorant of many things concerning the man." <note>Original Greek: ου γαρ... Who would doubt that in those four books by **Moeragenes** there were many things that could have demonstrated the character, morals, and actual deeds of **Apollonius**? 

Since the testimonies on which **Philostratus** relies are so weak—and indeed highly suspected of being false—it is easily seen what little weight the miracles attributed to **Apollonius** should have on the minds of readers. Yet even if we were to admit most of what **Philostratus** narrates (which cannot happen if we apply reason to our judgment), we could by no means persuade ourselves that miracles were performed by God for his sake. In the preceding sections, we have proven that this man most foolishly attributed omniscience to himself and boasted of having God as a perpetual companion, all to nourish and more widely spread the superstition raging everywhere...

...[prevented], yet they could not have been done. That is so; but we must first prove with certain and unquestionable evidence that these wonders actually occurred before we debate their causes and origins. Since there are so many arguments and testimonies showing that Damis could neither tell the truth nor had any desire to—being a foolish, gullible, simple, and deceitful man; that Philostratus embellished <note>original: "exornasse"</note> at his own whim a collection of things confusedly and foolishly heaped together and narrated; and that Apollonius himself was an *Impostor, a liar, and a fanatic man*, what forbids us from concluding that nothing was ever performed by him that exceeds human powers? But what was a *Magician* according to the opinion of that age? Clearly, he was a man who boasted that he enjoyed the intimate company of *Demons* and claimed he could perform extraordinary feats, yet in actual practice could achieve nothing. Anyone who examines the actions and lives of *Apuleius*, *Alexander* (whose tragedy <note>original: "τραγῳδίαν," referring to Alexander of Abonoteichus, a false prophet exposed by Lucian.</note> the very sharp Lucian recounts), *Iamblichus*, *Porphyry* <note>Neoplatonist philosophers often associated with theurgy and mystical practices.</note>, and others, will easily notice what kind of men those *Magicians* were.

Let *Francis* and his *Companions* follow next. We must now see with what degree of credibility the things said about their miracles rest. When we prove that the things told concerning the *Miracles of Christ* are true, we appeal to his disciples who were eyewitnesses <note>original Greek: "αὐτόπται" (autoptia)</note>; nor could they be so easily deceived, unless you were to say they had all *been deprived of the light of their eyes*. We assert, moreover, that they had no desire to deceive, which is clear from their entire *character* and life. They were indeed fishermen, simple men, unversed in literature; yet they were sincere, of sound mind, and not seized by any superstition. They recount things they saw a hundred times; they tell the circumstances of the deeds performed; nor do they appeal to perpetual visions and ecstasies; rather, with a certain natural simplicity <note>original: "ruditate," referring to a lack of formal rhetorical training or "roughness" of speech.</note>, they explain that they were fishermen, called by Christ to be witnesses of the things done by him, and to announce his most holy doctrine to everyone. They confess, furthermore, that they were equipped with unusual gifts—namely, the gift of tongues and the power of performing miracles—which they used to persuade men of the deeds and the divine origin of the most holy discipline. Let us now suppose, as *Bonaventure* <note>Saint Bonaventure (1221–1274), a major Scholastic theologian and the official biographer of St. Francis.</note> and others maintain, that there were twelve disciples of *Francis of Assisi* who were his constant companions in life and witnesses of his deeds. Even supposing this, however, we must admit that we cannot have faith in them because they narrate so many *ridiculous and absurd things*; and they themselves were so inept and dull-witted that other witnesses would be needed to prove that these men were even capable of telling the truth.

...the sky, and yet he is lifted up from the earth, and always looks downward; in this same way, it is necessary for us to be humbled. (page 53).

Brother Giles said to a certain person: "If you wish to enter the Religious life <note>original: "Religionem"; here referring to joining a monastic order</note> quickly, kill your parents—not with a physical sword, but with a spiritual one—because he who does not hate his father and mother cannot be a disciple of Christ." <note>This is a radical reference to Luke 14:26, emphasizing that devotion to God must come before even the closest family ties.</note> I shall add one example from the *Franciscan Antiquities* <note>original: "Antiquitat. Francisc." A collection of early records and legends of the Franciscan Order.</note>, page 164.

When Saint Louis, King of France, had decided to go on a seven-year pilgrimage to the various Holy Sanctuaries, and having heard the true reports and wonderful holiness of Brother Giles, he resolved in his heart to visit him by any means possible. Thus, during his journey, he turned aside to Perugia <note>original: "Perusium"</note>, where he had heard Brother Giles was staying. 

Arriving at the gate of the brothers like a poor, humble pilgrim, unknown and accompanied by only a few companions, he urgently requested to see Brother Giles, revealing nothing of his true rank to the gatekeeper <note>original: "portario"</note>. The gatekeeper went to Brother Giles, saying that a certain pilgrim was asking for him at the gate. Immediately, Brother Giles saw in the spirit that this was the King of France. Coming out of his cell as if intoxicated <note>original: "quasi ebrius"; in mystical tradition, this "spiritual intoxication" describes a state of divine ecstasy or overwhelming joy</note>, he ran with great speed to the gate. 

They both fell into a wonderful embrace and shared most devout kisses on bended knees, as if they had known each other through a lifelong friendship. Through these signs of charitable love, without uttering a single word to one another but remaining in total silence, they departed from each other. When the King was leaving, one of his companions was asked by the brothers who the man was who had embraced Brother Giles so lovingly. He replied that it was Lord Louis, King of France, who, while proceeding on his pilgrimage, had wished to see Brother Giles. After saying this, he and the King’s companions quickly departed.

*[...they departed]*, but the brothers, grieving that Brother Giles had spoken no good word to the said King, spoke to him, complaining in many ways: "O Brother Giles, why did you wish to say nothing to such a great King, who came from France to see you and hear you and receive some word from you?" And if we had wished to explain those things which we felt within through the service of vocal sound, on account of the defect of the human tongue—which cannot explain divine secrets except with the imagination of figures <note>meaning metaphorical or symbolic language</note>—that speech would have been for the desolation of both rather than for consolation. And therefore you should know that the King himself departed wonderfully consoled. To the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ."

...them even as much as possible; yet I argue that this does not prevent them from being able to provide testimony about things they saw with their own eyes. For nothing else is required for this except that a person is not blind or completely out of their mind. I respond that it is true that no unique sharpness of intellect is required to testify about a matter placed before one's eyes. However, while it is clearer than the midday sun that these most shameless men have accepted any legends narrated by others and have been driven mad by incredible superstition, who can doubt—since no actual evidence for the truth of these miracles is at hand—that they have been deceived a thousand times? Who could doubt that they have confused dreams with actual events? Indeed, casting aside all shame, they have babbled indiscriminately whatever came into their mouths <note>original: "in buccam venit"; a Latin idiom meaning to speak without thinking or to blather</note>.

From this source, they recite their trifles as if they were divine oracles: *Brother Giles <note>original: "Frater Ægidius"; Giles of Assisi (d. 1262), one of the first companions of St. Francis</note> said; Brother Anthony <note>original: "Frater Antonius"; St. Anthony of Padua (d. 1231), the most famous Franciscan preacher and miracle-worker</note> sees, etc.* They provide no circumstances regarding the event, the people involved, or the timing. If such things are to be accepted, then nothing has ever been said so foolishly or stupidly that it would not be considered sacred and divine. If the disciples of Christ had been so incompetent that they recounted the silliest things about themselves—if in their entire conduct they had acted like fanatics and highly superstitious men—who would finally believe the stupendous miracles they claim were performed by Christ? No one, certainly, except for a man who had a pumpkin for a brain <note>original: "pepo"; literally a large melon or pumpkin, used in Latin as a colloquialism for a blockhead or a fool</note>.

These things have been said in general about the witnesses and their character. Among the things told about Francis, the most extraordinary <note>original: "portentissimum"; while often meaning "wonderful," in this skeptical context it suggests something monstrous or incredibly unnatural</note> is undoubtedly what is related regarding the stigmata <term>stigmata: the appearance of wounds on the hands, feet, and side corresponding to those of Jesus during the Crucifixion</term> impressed upon his body. The matter, when examined in itself, shrinks so far from any appearance of probability that even several centuries of miracles could hardly convince me that it truly happened. *The earliest witness who tells that wonderful story is Cardinal Bonaventure. He was born in the year 1221 and died in the year 1274; however, Francis died in the year 1226. He could not, therefore, have been a witness to such an unusual event.*

But perhaps he heard the story told by others, unless he invented it himself. Thus, the entire weight of the narrative returns to the authors who told this wonderful and unusual thing to *Bonaventure*. Even if we assume that a disciple of Francis told it to *Bonaventure*, the question remains once more whether trust should be placed in disciples so dull and foolish as those we heard about above. *On page 8 of the Alcoran* <note>original: "Alcorani"; referring to the "Alcoranus Franciscanorum" or "The Koran of the Franciscans," a mocking title used by critics for the "Liber Conformitatum," a 14th-century book that claimed Francis was a second Christ</note> it is asserted that *Bonaventure* received that story from those who saw it, *and touched it, and confirmed it by oath.*

*But we heard above from the same Alcoran on page 41 that Brother Leo was alone with Francis on Mount La Verna <note>original: "monte Alverne"; the mountain in Tuscany where Francis is said to have received the stigmata in 1224</note>, and to him alone was it granted to touch the wounds.* This, as we have heard, is denied in another place; on page 235 in the works of *Bosquier* <note>Philippe Bosquier (1562–1636), a Franciscan author known for his ornate sermons</note>, it is said that nine people saw the wounds. But who lied—Brother Leo, or those many who told the story to *Bonaventure*, or *Bonaventure* himself? Let the ghost <note>original: "manes"; refers to the spirit or shade of the deceased</note> of *Blessed Francis* explain it to us. *On page 197*, the testimony of the *Blessed Mary* and the Angels is invoked to prove that most miraculous of miracles. But these testimonies hold no weight among those skilled in the historical art. *On page 198, the Alcoran mentions the Bull* <note>Referring to a Papal Bull, an official decree issued by the Pope to authenticate the miracle</note>

## *Of Pope Gregory IX regarding the stigmatization of Blessed Francis.*

How much weight those testimonies carry is easy to judge: I do not doubt that a Bull <term>Bull: an official papal decree, named after the "bulla" or lead seal attached to it</term> was issued by the *Pope* to confirm such a wonderful and unusual thing. For it is well known how much influence superstition and the impudence of the Popes had at that time—as well as in our own. And if the *Pope* could reach such a level of madness <note>original: "dementiæ"</note> as to enroll *Francis* among the number of the Saints, he could certainly also issue a Bull. We shall deal with this argument in the following chapter. Therefore, all belief regarding the impressed stigmata rests upon the authority of *Brother Leo* and *Francis*. As for what kind of man that *Brother Leo* was, we have heard in part above, and we shall provide one or two further examples here. From page 40 of the *Alcoran* <note>original: "Alcorani"; referring to the "Alcoran of the Franciscans," a satirical Protestant work by Erasmus Alber which mocked Franciscan legends by comparing them to the Quran</note>:

> When *Brother Leo* did not find *Blessed Francis* in his cell, he saw him raised so high in the air <term>levitatio: the miraculous lifting of a human body into the air</term> that he was able to touch his feet; while kissing and embracing them, he said: "God be merciful to me, a sinner, and through the merits of this most holy man, grant that I may find your mercy."

In the *Franciscan Antiquities* <note>original: "Antiquit. Francisc."</note> from page 210 up to page 230, examples are read of the supreme stupidity <note>original: "stoliditatis"</note> of this *Leo*, who ought rather to be called an *Ass* <note>original: "Asinus"</note>. Thus, on page 216:

> Because *Saint Francis*—a lover of that glorious innocence which adorns the body, leads the soul to grace, and leads to glory—perceived in *Brother Leo* a great purity and dovelike innocence, he more frequently took him as his *Companion*, and admitted him more often to his secrets, both by day and by night. For this reason, among all the *Companions of the Holy Father*, the one who knew most about his secrets and his wonders was the aforementioned *Brother Leo*. For he himself frequently saw him raised in the air. He

He also heard him frequently speaking with Christ, and with the Blessed Virgin, and with the Angels. Moreover, he saw a fiery light descending from heaven upon **St. Francis**, and heard a voice from that very light speaking with him. One day, while they were walking along together, he saw a most beautiful cross preceding the face of **St. Francis**, with Christ hanging upon it. That cross was of such splendor that it not only illuminated **St. Francis’s** face, but also illuminated and adorned the air all around, and **Brother Leo** saw it in a clear light.

It would be tiresome to write more. You are to trust this man, then, in his narration of a most unusual matter: indeed, you could easily persuade such a man that circles are squares, and that the <term>iaëra</term> <note>original: "iaëra"; likely a variant of "aëra," meaning the air</note> is full of winged oxen. This miracle, moreover, is of such a nature that if it had truly happened, and had been confirmed by trustworthy witnesses, its fame would have been spread through all lands. None of the historians who lived at that time and committed noteworthy things to paper would have passed it over in silence.

*This is the single point we wish to establish.* Therefore, the credibility of the entire narrative rests upon the authority of *Francis*, who told his disciples that this vision had occurred to him. 3° Furthermore, we cannot safely trust him, not only because of his clearly foolish and fanatical character—and because he told countless stories about himself (if one believes the *Legends* <note>The "Legends" refer to the medieval hagiographies or official lives of the saints.</note>) which are plainly senseless and unbelievable—but also because the event itself could not have happened, as it is contrary to God and the *Most Holy Religion*. If someone were to shout a hundred times that it was revealed to him through a vision that *Jesus* is not the true *Messiah*, no one would believe him; instead, he would be regarded as *insane* or an *Impostor*.

Therefore, for this reason alone, he was able to reject it. 4th. But the *Most Learned Man* asks how it happened that men accepted such an unusual thing. But this argument would prove more than was intended to be proven, and thus it proves nothing. If this way of arguing were true, it would follow that all follies and all fabricated miracles—which no one at the time they were said to have happened contradicted—must be accepted as the most certain truths. How many tasteless fables were finally outlawed in the *16th Century* which the Monks used to accept as if they were Oracles? If anyone considers the time in which *Francis* lived—if they place before themselves the superstition raging everywhere, the ignorance, the *Authority of the Popes*, and the suppression of all free examination of Religion—

...who does not know that every sacred shrine and every monastery claims a divine origin for itself? Therefore, in my opinion, the argument based on the *Silence of Bonaventure* <note>Saint Bonaventure (1221–1274), the Minister General of the Franciscans who wrote the "Legenda Maior," the official biography of St. Francis.</note> remains solid. This man was a most zealous devotee of *Francis*; he gathered up every fable, every foolish deed, and every portent he could scrape together and committed them to paper. What reason, then, would he have for suppressing this unusual vision in silence? He recounted the story of the *stigmata* <note>The physical wounds corresponding to the crucifixion of Jesus, said to have appeared on Francis's body in 1224.</note>, which is said to have occurred the following year; why, then, was he so profoundly silent regarding this vision? Had others writing at the same time composed histories of Christian events, they might well have failed to mention these things, and in that case, nothing could be safely inferred from their silence. But *Bonaventure* made a deliberate effort and used singular zeal to collect everything that could bolster the authority of *Francis*. Thus, a solid argument regarding the worthlessness of that vision can be drawn from his silence.

### *The Mandate of Munio, Master of the Order of Friars Preachers, to Friar Theodoric of Apolda, in which we have changed nothing.*

To his beloved brother in Christ, Theodoric of Apolda <note>A Dominican friar and author (c. 1228–1298) tasked with writing the official biography of St. Dominic.</note> of the Erfurt house in the province of Germany, Brother Munio <note>Munio of Zamora, the seventh Master General of the Dominican Order.</note>, Master of the Order though unworthy, sends greetings and a continuous increase of heavenly graces. I wish, moreover, that your Prior, whoever he may be at the time, assist you with timely help, counsel, and comfort. Farewell and pray for me. Given in Orvieto <note>original: "Urbe Veteri." Hence, the first *Authors* of the miracles attributed to *Dominic* and *Francis* <note>Saint Francis of Assisi (1181–1226), founder of the Franciscan Order and contemporary of Dominic.</note> were not only credulous, but were also fraudulent *Impostores*. 

It is strange, however, that the *Learned Men* whom I just mentioned reject *one* or *another* miracle while admitting all the rest. Truly, I see no reason why, if *one* or *two* are admitted, I should reject the others. When *Learned Men* complain about the credulity of witnesses regarding a single miracle, they show by that very fact that they have little trust in those witnesses. But if those witnesses, out of excessive credulity, could admit or invent one false thing, what reason is there to doubt that they did this in most or all cases? 

If, compelled by the authority of the disciples of *Christ*—or rather by their faithfulness and zeal for the truth—I admit a true miracle (for example, the one performed at the wedding in *Cana* <note>original: "Cananeæ in nuptiis." For as long as I believe on the one hand that miracles are possible, and on the other hand am fully persuaded of the faith and piety of the disciples who testify to them, there is no reason why I should prefer *one* over another, even if one seems more or less unusual than the rest.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Pedro de Ribadeneira’s biography of Ignatius Loyola. ...distinguished by divine operations. He <note>Ribadeneira</note> responds: Just as He <note>God</note> alone is able to effect these things, so He alone knows in what place, at what time, and through whose prayers miracles are to be performed.

He then strives to prove, by the introduction of examples and by passages of **Holy Scripture**, that it is not necessary for this to happen: "Neither did all **Holy Men**," he says, "excel in miracles; nor did those who surpassed others in the magnitude or abundance of miracles for that reason exceed the rest in holiness. For the holiness of each person is to be judged not by signs, but by charity." 

He proves, moreover, from **Holy Writ**, that the gift of miracles is sometimes granted to false teachers. "I would say these things," he says, "not to diminish the power of miracles, but so that the prudent Reader may understand that the whole matter is to be committed to God, who distributes His gifts to each person as He wills." 

He <note>God</note> could, according to His hidden wisdom, have granted this to our weakness, so that we might never be able to boast of miracles; He could have done it for our benefit, so that, because the Author of our institute <note>Ignatius Loyola</note> was less illustrious, we might take our name from **Jesus** rather than from him; and so that our sacred title might warn us never to turn our eyes away from Him: whom we ought to worship and imitate not only as the common liberator and Prince of the human race, but also as our chief leader, decorating this <term>least society</term> <note>original: *minimam hanc societatem*; a standard Jesuit expression of humility regarding their Order</note> with the glorious title of His name. 

He could also have attributed this to the times, in which these miracles are not necessary. Finally, from the marvelous progress of the society, he concludes that God has sufficiently provided for the **Authority** and **Holiness of Ignatius**. 

**Ribadeneira** published another edition in 1587, in which he again maintains that no miracles were performed by **Ignatius**; although in the preface he says: "Many things [have come] to me..."

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Pedro de Ribadeneira’s biography of Ignatius Loyola. Following the previous page’s discussion on why miracles might not be necessary for holiness, Ribadeneira here explains why he eventually chose to include them in later editions after initially omitting them.</meta>

...I judged it necessary to add. First, certain new things which, after the book was printed, most serious men—those very familiar with Ignatius and his intimate associates from before the <term>society</term> <note>The Society of Jesus, or the Jesuits</note> was founded—reported to us as eyewitnesses about Ignatius himself; then other things, which were previously doubtful to me, and which I later found to be certain after a diligent investigation. Finally, there is nothing regarding miracles in the Lyon edition of the year 1595, published by Jean Gesselin. 

But at last, the scene changed. For the same Ribadeneira published a third edition in 1610, in which he brought forward a great abundance of miracles performed by Ignatius. Since the Jesuit <note>Ribadeneira</note> easily foresaw that there would be many who would wonder why mention of miracles was only being made at that late time, he thought this doubt should be addressed; hence in Chapter 18 of the final edition, he says:

> Because in the last chapter of the fifth book we dealt briefly with miracles, as if he had performed none, or as if they were not necessary to demonstrate his holiness, I have now decided to set them forth a little more extensively—not all of them, indeed (for the matter would run on too long), but at least a part of those which God deigned to effect through His servant. For although when I first wrote his life in Latin in the year 1572, I had known of several other miracles performed by him, they were not yet so certain and well-investigated to me that I could persuade myself to publish them to the public; but later, after the public inquiries regarding his <term>canonization</term> <note>original: *in divos relatione*; literally, "enrollment among the gods," a classical Latin expression for being declared a saint</note> were held, they were confirmed by serious and suitable witnesses. Indeed, so that God might exalt His servant on earth, He deigns to honor him with such frequent miracles daily that I consider it my duty to commit some to writing here, taken from the public records.

From these facts, Pierre Bayle <note>original: "P. Baylius"; Pierre Bayle (1647–1706) was a French philosopher and critic famous for his *Dictionnaire Historique et Critique*, a seminal work of the early Enlightenment.</note> concludes in his *Dictionary* <note>original: "Lexico"</note> that the miracles attributed to Loyola are doubtful and false. > *Let us conclude from this (he says) that the miracles of Saint Ignatius are not things that his friends taught Ribadeneira during the fifteen years separating the two editions, nor was this author able to emerge from uncertainty during that interval of time. There was undoubtedly nothing among the things of which he was not then perfectly sure for which he sought certainty more carefully than the miracles of his Apostle: since, therefore, he continued to say in the edition of 1587 that the blessed Ignatius had performed no miracles, it necessarily follows that his most exact inquiries had taught him nothing certain on this subject. Furthermore, would a Jesuit who knew in the year 1572 that his founder had performed miracles—and who only abstained from inserting them into a public work because his knowledge of them was not what it should be when such facts are printed—would he confess that his founder performed no miracles? Would he reason about that with such study? Would he answer objections so precisely?*

Therefore, no more probable cause for his silence regarding the miracles can be offered than that Ribadeneira was convinced that everything said about them rested either on uncertain human rumors and talk, or that absolutely nothing had ever been done by him. The worship of the Gods, says Cicero <note>A quote from Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman philosopher. Enlightenment-era writers often cited him to show that even "natural reason" without the Bible could recognize pure worship.</note>, is the best, and likewise the most chaste, most holy, and most full of piety, when we venerate them always with a pure, intact, and uncorrupted mind and voice.* That worship requires above all that we bid farewell to the wicked desires of the soul, and that we pluck the roots of vices from the heart.

These things are known by reason alone. But if the **Popes** had ever measured the worship—which they wished to recommend to men as *Divine* through their precepts and examples, namely that of *Francis, Loyola, and Dominic* <note>Saint Francis of Assisi, Ignatius of Loyola, and Saint Dominic, the founders of the Franciscan, Jesuit, and Dominican orders.</note>—against the standard of right reason, it would have been impossible for them to persuade themselves that God Himself had performed miracles to establish that kind of worship. Indeed, they would have believed that even without miracles, such behavior could not be pleasing to Him. Therefore, the error of those **Popes** was not only conquerable <term>vincibilis (vincible error): A theological concept referring to an error or ignorance that a person could have overcome if they had exercised reasonable care or diligence.</term>, but was also of such a kind that could [hardly] be committed without either extreme ignorance or wickedness...

I have no doubt that many people, having read those things which we have said above regarding the life, character, and teachings of **Francis**, **Dominic**, and **Loyola**, <note>Francis of Assisi, Dominic de Guzmán, and Ignatius of Loyola—the founders of the Franciscan, Dominican, and Jesuit orders.</note> will wonder by what reasoning it could have happened that men so foolish and superstitious were entered into the number of the **Saints**, and held in such high esteem to this very day. *Socrates* did as much as he could to recommend natural religion <term>Natural Religion: A system of belief based on reason and the observation of the natural world, rather than on supernatural revelation.</term> to his *Athenians*, and to criticize and correct the corrupt morals of the city. *Francis* and the others, however, were able to perceive everywhere that the most pure worship of God was clearly contaminated by the foulest superstition, and that people were utterly ignorant of the true Religion announced through *Christ* and the *Apostles*. They would point to the *Papal Bull Unigeniti* <term>Unigeniti: A controversial 1713 papal bull issued by Pope Clement XI to condemn Jansenism, which sparked intense political and religious debate in France over papal authority versus local church rights</term> as an *illustrious example* of this. This is how I believe *wise men* and *seekers of truth* would respond. I am not someone who believes that I could, by any measure, be compared in *Learning* or *sharpness of mind* to such *Great Men*. However, from what I can see, the reasons they provide are not of *great weight*. The sum of their entire argument boils down to this: *errors and superstition* should only be confronted when it is believed such a thing can be done *without fear or tumult*. 

But if this is to be accepted as an *Axiom*, then not only the course of *True Learning*, but also all progress in *piety* and the *work of Religion* will be *hindered* <note>original: "sufflaminabitur," a metaphor for clogging a wheel or applying a brake</note>. Our efforts are blocked by the *Decrees of Emperors*, the *Cruelty of Prefects*, and the *rage of the petty priests*: therefore, we must wait until *superstition collapses under its own weight*," etc.

But if the followers of the most holy teachings <note>The author likely refers to the Apostles or the early Church fathers</note> had reasoned in this way, that most foul superstition would never have been abolished. They can learn what a noble impulse can achieve from our own example—we who made a secession <note>The author identifies as a Protestant, referring to the Reformation as a "secession" from the Roman Church</note> because of the intolerable yoke of servitude.
